stem_en: Who are Australia's first inhabitants?
options_en: The first settlers who arrived from Great Britain
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
The European explorers who mapped the coastline
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are Australia's first inhabitants.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which group has lived in Australia for the longest time?
options_en: Free settlers who came from Great Britain and Ireland
Explorers who charted the coastline of Australia
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
explanation_en: The booklet's section on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples describes them as Australia's first inhabitants.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: The cultures and traditions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are
options_en: among the newest cultures in the Pacific region
based mainly on traditions brought from Europe
the oldest continuous cultures in the world
explanation_en: Part 1 says Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures is correct?
options_en: They are the world's oldest continuous cultures
They began after European settlement in 1788
They were brought to Australia from Asia in 1901
explanation_en: The booklet describes these cultures as the oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world, long before European settlement.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which parts of Australia are Aboriginal people historically from?
options_en: The islands north of Queensland only
The mainland and Tasmania
New Zealand and the nearby Pacific islands
explanation_en: Part 1 states that Aboriginal people are historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Where are Torres Strait Islander people historically from?
options_en: Islands in the Bass Strait between Tasmania and the mainland
The islands off the south-western coast of Western Australia
The islands north of Queensland, towards Papua New Guinea
explanation_en: The booklet says Torres Strait Islander people are from islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: The Torres Strait Islands lie near the northern tip of which state?
options_en: Western Australia
Queensland
New South Wales
explanation_en: Part 1 places the Torres Strait Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: According to the archaeological record, how long ago did Aboriginal peoples arrive in Australia?
options_en: Somewhere between 40,000 and 65,000 years ago
Roughly 2,000 years ago
Only a few years before the First Fleet
explanation_en: Part 1 notes that the archaeological record points to Aboriginal peoples arriving between 65,000 and 40,000 years ago, while their own creation stories begin with the beginning of time.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Aboriginal peoples believe their creation stories begin
options_en: at the beginning of time
with the arrival of the First Fleet
at Federation in 1901
explanation_en: The booklet explains that Aboriginal peoples' creation stories commence with the beginning of time.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which is correct about Aboriginal peoples and the creation stories of this land?
options_en: They believe the stories were brought from Europe
They believe they are central to those stories
They believe the stories began in 1788
explanation_en: Part 1 says Aboriginal peoples believe they are central to the creation stories of this land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: The age-old beliefs and traditions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
options_en: still guide them today
ended at Federation in 1901
are no longer practised anywhere
explanation_en: Part 1 states that these age-old beliefs and traditions still guide Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples today.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: How do Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples express their connection with the land?
options_en: Through written laws and treaties
Through stories, art and dance
Through parliamentary debates
explanation_en: The booklet says their deep connection with the land is expressed in their stories, art and dance.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have a deep connection with
options_en: the land
the British monarchy
the city of Canberra
explanation_en: Part 1 describes the deep connection Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have with the land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Indigenous cultures in Australia are
options_en: identical across the whole country
diverse and part of the national identity
separate from Australia's national identity
explanation_en: Part 1 says Indigenous cultures are diverse and an important part of Australia's national identity.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which is true of Indigenous cultures in Australia?
options_en: There is a single Indigenous culture shared by all
Indigenous cultures were brought here from Europe
There are many different Indigenous cultures
explanation_en: The booklet describes Indigenous cultures as diverse, meaning there are many different cultures across Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: About how many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are valued alongside English?
options_en: More than 100
Fewer than 10
Exactly one
explanation_en: The section on the nation of Australia says more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are valued alongside English.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are
options_en: not permitted in public
the official national language
valued alongside English
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that English is the national language, but other languages, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, are also valued.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: In Australia, 'Indigenous' refers to
options_en: Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Australians
people who were born in Australia to parents who migrated here
the earliest free settlers who came from Great Britain and Ireland
explanation_en: The glossary defines Indigenous as the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Indigenous Australians are also known as
options_en: the passengers of the First Fleet
the First Peoples of this country
the founding colonists of New South Wales
explanation_en: The glossary says Indigenous Australians are the First Peoples of this country.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A Welcome to Country is performed by
options_en: the mayor or another member of the local council
a local Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian
the Governor-General or the governor of the host state
explanation_en: Part 1 describes a Welcome to Country as a cultural practice carried out by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: What does a Welcome to Country do?
options_en: Grants visitors the legal right to Australian citizenship
Formally opens each new sitting of the Australian Parliament
Welcomes visitors to the custodians' traditional land
explanation_en: The booklet explains that a Welcome to Country welcomes visitors to the traditional land of the local custodian.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Traditionally, a Welcome to Country was performed so that visitors
options_en: had a safe and protected journey on that land
paid a fee to the custodians before entering the land
could purchase land from the local custodians
explanation_en: Part 1 says a Welcome to Country was traditionally performed to ensure visitors had a safe and protected journey during their time on that land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Visitors are welcomed onto traditional land with a Welcome to Country. Traditionally, what was this meant to give them?
options_en: A safe and protected stay on that land
A written record of their names kept by the custodians
Permission to buy land from the custodians
explanation_en: The booklet's section on traditions says the practice was performed to ensure visitors had a safe and protected journey.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which of these is a form a Welcome to Country can take?
options_en: A fireworks display
A military parade
A smoking ceremony
explanation_en: Part 1 lists songs, dances, smoking ceremonies and speeches as forms a Welcome to Country can take.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: A Welcome to Country speech may be given in
options_en: Latin or another ancient language
traditional language or English
written form only, never spoken
explanation_en: The booklet says a Welcome to Country can include speeches in traditional language or English.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: In the running order of an event, a Welcome to Country usually comes
options_en: first, to open the event
last, to close the event
after the main speeches end
explanation_en: Part 1 says a Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings to open an event.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: You attend a community event. When would you expect a Welcome to Country?
options_en: In the middle, after the lunch break
At the end, to close the event
At the start, to open the event
explanation_en: The booklet explains that a Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings at an event.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: An event organiser who is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander wants to perform a Welcome to Country. Is this appropriate?
options_en: Yes, anyone who organises the event is able to perform it
Yes, as long as they live in the local area
No, only a custodian of the local region performs it
explanation_en: Part 1 is clear that a Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: The Master of Ceremonies at a meeting wants to open proceedings. Which can they deliver?
options_en: An Acknowledgement of Country
A Welcome to Country
Either, as long as they live nearby
explanation_en: The booklet says anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country, but a Welcome to Country is performed only by a local Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: An Acknowledgement of Country recognises that
options_en: the gathering has received formal approval from the government
the gathering is on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land
the land is owned by the Commonwealth
explanation_en: Part 1 says an Acknowledgement of Country recognises that the gathering is on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: In an Acknowledgement of Country, respect is paid to
options_en: the Prime Minister and the premiers of all six Australian states
the founders and officers of the local council
Traditional Custodians, particularly Elders past and present
explanation_en: The booklet explains that an Acknowledgement of Country pays respect to Traditional Custodians, particularly Elders past and present.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Recognising that a gathering is on Aboriginal land and paying respect to Elders is called
options_en: a Welcome to Country ceremony
a traditional smoking ceremony
an Acknowledgement of Country
explanation_en: Part 1 defines an Acknowledgement of Country as recognising the land and paying respect to Traditional Custodians and Elders.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Is there a restriction on who may give an Acknowledgement of Country?
options_en: Yes, only an Elder may give one
Yes, only a government official may give one
No, anyone may give one
explanation_en: The booklet states plainly that anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: A teacher who is not Indigenous wants to open assembly by acknowledging the Traditional Custodians. Can they?
options_en: Yes, anyone can give an Acknowledgement of Country
No, only a custodian of the local region can do this
No, this is only allowed at government events
explanation_en: Part 1 says anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country, unlike a Welcome to Country.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which statement about who may perform these two protocols is correct?
options_en: Both can be given by anyone who attends the event
Only a Welcome to Country needs a local custodian
Both must be given by an Aboriginal Elder
explanation_en: Part 1 says a Welcome to Country is performed by a local Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian, while anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: At a meeting, an Acknowledgement of Country is generally delivered by
options_en: the Chair or Master of Ceremonies
the youngest person at the meeting
a politician visiting the meeting
explanation_en: Part 1 says that at meetings and events this is generally done by the Chair or Master of Ceremonies.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: At a meeting, when is an Acknowledgement of Country usually given?
options_en: During the closing remarks and thanks
During the Welcome and Housekeeping
During the formal voting procedure
explanation_en: The booklet says an Acknowledgement of Country is usually delivered as part of the Welcome and Housekeeping at meetings and events.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Why are Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country performed?
options_en: To satisfy a legal requirement that applies to all public gatherings
To raise funds for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community groups
As a mark of respect towards Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
explanation_en: Part 1 says these practices are performed to show respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which statement about these two protocols is correct?
options_en: Both must be performed by an elected official of the government
Both are ways of showing respect for Australia's First Peoples
Both are required by law at every event
explanation_en: The booklet explains that Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country are performed to show respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: At your citizenship ceremony, you may be welcomed by
options_en: a representative of the traditional owners of the land in your area
an official representative of the United Kingdom's government in Australia
the leader of the opposition in your state
explanation_en: The booklet's description of the citizenship ceremony says you may be welcomed by a representative of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander traditional owners of the land.
guideRef: A message to you — The Australian citizenship ceremony

stem_en: When you become a citizen at your ceremony, you pledge your loyalty to
options_en: the Prime Minister of the day
your own state or territory
Australia and its people
explanation_en: Part 1 opens by saying that at the citizenship ceremony you pledge your loyalty to Australia and its people.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia and its people

stem_en: Why should new citizens understand Australia's Indigenous heritage?
options_en: Because it is needed to apply for an Australian passport
Because it decides which state they may live in
Because they pledge loyalty to Australia and its people
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that because you pledge loyalty to Australia and its people, you should understand its community and population, including its Indigenous heritage.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia and its people

stem_en: Australia has developed into
options_en: a stable and successful multicultural nation
a nation with a single culture shared by everyone
a colony governed from Great Britain
explanation_en: Part 1 says Australia has developed into a stable and successful multicultural nation.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia and its people

stem_en: Which group is historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania?
options_en: Torres Strait Islander people
Aboriginal people
Papua New Guinean people
explanation_en: Part 1 distinguishes Aboriginal people, from mainland Australia and Tasmania, from Torres Strait Islander people, who are from islands north of Queensland.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Which protocol is performed by a custodian welcoming visitors to their traditional land?
options_en: An Acknowledgement of Country
A Welcome to Country
A citizenship pledge
explanation_en: The booklet defines a Welcome to Country as a custodian of the local region welcoming visitors to their traditional land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Torres Strait Islander people come from islands that lie between northern Queensland and which country?
options_en: Indonesia
Papua New Guinea
New Zealand
explanation_en: The section on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples places the Torres Strait Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Besides the Traditional Custodians and their Elders, who else is paid respect in an Acknowledgement of Country?
options_en: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people at the gathering
The Governor-General and each of the state governors
The organisers, sponsors and caterers of the event
explanation_en: The protocols section says an Acknowledgement of Country also pays respect to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples who are present at the gathering.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which of these is NOT a form a Welcome to Country can take?
options_en: A traditional dance
A smoking ceremony
A flag-raising ceremony
explanation_en: The protocols section lists songs, dances, smoking ceremonies and speeches in traditional language or English; a flag-raising is not among them.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: A company opens its annual meeting with no Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian present. How can the Chair still open respectfully?
options_en: By performing a Welcome to Country on the custodians' behalf
By delivering an Acknowledgement of Country
By postponing the meeting until a custodian can attend
explanation_en: Anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country, and at meetings this is generally done by the Chair or Master of Ceremonies, as the protocols section explains.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which of these is true of an Acknowledgement of Country but not of a Welcome to Country?
options_en: It welcomes visitors onto traditional land
Only a custodian of the local region may perform it
Anyone may deliver it
explanation_en: The protocols section says a Welcome to Country is performed by a local custodian, whereas an Acknowledgement of Country can be delivered by anyone.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: A conference program places the Welcome to Country after the main speech on day two. Where does it usually belong?
options_en: At the start, as the first item
At the close of the final day of the conference
Anywhere in the program, as the organisers decide
explanation_en: The protocols section says a Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings used to open an event.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Besides the mainland, which island state are Aboriginal people historically from?
options_en: Tasmania
The Torres Strait Islands
New Zealand's South Island
explanation_en: The section on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples says Aboriginal people are historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania.
guideRef: Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

stem_en: Three events open in different ways. Which opening is an Acknowledgement of Country?
options_en: A local Elder performing a smoking ceremony to greet guests at a festival
A custodian welcoming visitors in traditional language at a conference
A school principal recognising the Traditional Custodians before assembly
explanation_en: A Welcome to Country is performed by a custodian of the local land, while recognising the Traditional Custodians is an Acknowledgement of Country, which anyone can deliver, as the protocols section explains.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: What is usually the first item of proceedings when an event opens?
options_en: The national anthem
A Welcome to Country
A speech by the Master of Ceremonies
explanation_en: The protocols section says a Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings to open an event.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

stem_en: Which term covers both Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples?
options_en: Custodian
Elder
Indigenous
explanation_en: The glossary defines 'Indigenous' as the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: European settlement of Australia began when the First Fleet arrived on
options_en: 26 January 1788
26 January 1901
25 April 1915
explanation_en: Part 1 says European settlement started when the First Fleet arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: The First Fleet that began European settlement sailed from
options_en: the Netherlands
Great Britain
Portugal
explanation_en: The booklet's section on early European settlement says the First Fleet arrived from Great Britain in 1788.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: From which countries did Australia's early free settlers mostly come?
options_en: Great Britain and Ireland
Germany and the Netherlands
China and Southeast Asia
explanation_en: Part 1 says early free settlers came from Great Britain and Ireland.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: Australia's recent history, culture and politics have been strongly influenced by which heritage?
options_en: French and Spanish
British and Irish
Dutch and Portuguese
explanation_en: The booklet notes that Australia's British and Irish heritage has had a major influence on its recent history, culture and politics.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: What did the Australian colonies form when they joined together in 1901?
options_en: Six fully independent nations with their own kings
A federation called the Commonwealth of Australia
One large colony ruled directly from Great Britain
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that in 1901 the separate colonies were united into a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: What name was given to the new nation formed in 1901?
options_en: The Commonwealth of Australia
The Colony of New South Wales
The United States of Australia
explanation_en: Part 1 says the federation of states created in 1901 was called the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: Which national institutions were established under the new Constitution at Federation?
options_en: The state police forces and local councils
The national parliament, government and High Court
The Australian Defence Force and the Reserve Bank of Australia
explanation_en: Part 1 says that at Federation in 1901 the national parliament, government and High Court were established under the new Australian Constitution.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: When was the High Court of Australia established?
options_en: When the First Fleet arrived in 1788
After the 1967 Referendum had been passed by voters
At Federation in 1901, under the Constitution
explanation_en: The booklet explains that the national democratic institutions, including the High Court, were established under the new Constitution in 1901.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: After the 1967 Referendum, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were
options_en: given their own separate national parliament
required to move away from the capital cities
included in official population estimates
explanation_en: Part 1 says it was only after a Referendum in 1967 that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were included in official estimates of the population.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: In which year was the Referendum after which Indigenous Australians were counted in population estimates?
explanation_en: The booklet says Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were included in official population estimates only after the 1967 Referendum.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: In recent years, Australia's migration and refugee programs have brought people here to
options_en: work here for a short time and then leave
escape poverty, war or persecution
take over the running of the state parliaments
explanation_en: Part 1 says recent migration and refugee programs have brought people to join family, make a new life, or escape poverty, war or persecution.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: What effect does Australia's diverse society have?
options_en: It strengthens Australia's connection to the world
It isolates Australia from other countries around the world
It weakens the national economy over the long term
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that Australia's diverse and prosperous society enhances its connection to the world.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: Alongside celebrating diversity, what kind of nation does Australia aim to build?
options_en: A cohesive and unified one
One where communities stay separate
One with a single culture for everyone
explanation_en: The booklet says that while Australia celebrates diversity, it also aims to build a cohesive and unified nation.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: Which language is Australia's national language?
options_en: Mandarin
Spanish
English
explanation_en: Part 1 states that Australia's national language is English and that it is part of the national identity.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: Why should migrants learn and use English?
options_en: Because speaking other languages is not allowed
Because it is required before they can vote
To help them take part in Australian society
explanation_en: Part 1 says migrants should learn and use English to help them participate in Australian society.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: Besides English, how many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are valued in Australia?
options_en: About 20
Fewer than 10
More than 100
explanation_en: Part 1 says other languages are valued, including more than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.
guideRef: Part 1 — The nation of Australia

stem_en: How many states and mainland territories does Australia have?
options_en: Six states and two mainland territories
Eight states and no mainland territories
Five states and three mainland territories
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Commonwealth of Australia is made up of six states and two mainland territories.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Which of these is a territory rather than a state?
options_en: Tasmania
Northern Territory
Queensland
explanation_en: The booklet lists six states, including Tasmania and Queensland, and two mainland territories, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Australia's national capital city is
options_en: Sydney
Canberra
Melbourne
explanation_en: Part 1 states that Canberra is Australia's capital city.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Sydney is the capital city of
options_en: Western Australia
New South Wales
South Australia
explanation_en: The table of states and capitals in Part 1 shows Sydney as the capital of New South Wales.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: The capital city of Victoria is
options_en: Melbourne
Hobart
Adelaide
explanation_en: Part 1 lists Melbourne as the capital of Victoria.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Which city is the capital of Queensland?
options_en: Brisbane
Adelaide
Canberra
explanation_en: Part 1 lists Brisbane as the capital of Queensland.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Perth is the capital of which state?
options_en: Western Australia
Northern Territory
South Australia
explanation_en: The booklet's table of capitals shows Perth as the capital of Western Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: The capital city of South Australia is
options_en: Adelaide
Perth
Melbourne
explanation_en: Part 1 lists Adelaide as the capital of South Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Hobart is the capital of
options_en: Victoria
Tasmania
the Australian Capital Territory
explanation_en: Part 1 lists Hobart as the capital of Tasmania.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Which city is the capital of the Australian Capital Territory?
options_en: Brisbane
Canberra
Adelaide
explanation_en: The booklet lists Canberra as the capital of the Australian Capital Territory, as well as the national capital.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: The capital city of the Northern Territory is
options_en: Darwin
Brisbane
Perth
explanation_en: Part 1 lists Darwin as the capital of the Northern Territory.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: The British established their first Australian colony in
options_en: Western Australia
South Australia
New South Wales
explanation_en: The booklet's section on the states says New South Wales was the first colony established by the British.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Australia's largest city is
options_en: Melbourne
Canberra
Sydney
explanation_en: Part 1 says Sydney, the capital of New South Wales, is the nation's largest city.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which is the smallest of the mainland states?
options_en: Victoria
Tasmania
South Australia
explanation_en: The booklet says Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states; Tasmania is the smallest state overall but is an island.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: The Melbourne Cricket Ground and the 12 Apostles are icons of which state?
options_en: New South Wales
Victoria
Western Australia
explanation_en: Part 1 lists the Melbourne Cricket Ground, the 12 Apostles and the Royal Exhibition Building as Victorian icons.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: The Great Barrier Reef runs along the eastern coast of
options_en: New South Wales
Western Australia
Queensland
explanation_en: Part 1 says the world-famous Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland's eastern coast.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which is Australia's second largest state?
options_en: Western Australia
New South Wales
Queensland
explanation_en: The booklet says Queensland is the second largest state, while Western Australia is the largest.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which state has tropical rainforests in some areas and an inland that is often dry?
options_en: Western Australia
New South Wales
Queensland
explanation_en: Part 1 describes Queensland as having tropical rainforests, temperate coastal areas and an often dry inland.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which is Australia's largest state?
options_en: Western Australia
Queensland

South Australia

Tasmania

Victoria
South Australia

stem_en: Port Arthur, the Bay of Fires and Cradle Mountain are icons of

Tasmania
Northern Territory

Sydney and Melbourne

The High Court of Australia and Parliament House
The Melbourne Cricket Ground and the 12 Apostles

stem_en: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of

the Northern Territory
South Australia

a national vote to change the Australian Constitution
the union of colonies into one nation

stem_en: An 'icon' is

a well-known image, such as the Opera House
a public holiday celebrated in every state and territory

stem_en: In which year did the gold rush begin in New South Wales and Victoria?
explanation_en: The section on the early days of European settlement says a gold rush began in 1851 when gold was found in New South Wales and Victoria.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: In which two colonies did the gold rush of 1851 begin?
options_en: New South Wales and Victoria
Queensland and Tasmania
South Australia and Western Australia
explanation_en: The early settlement section names the colonies of New South Wales and Victoria as the places where gold was discovered in 1851.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: Who were the first large group of migrants to Australia who did not come from Europe?
options_en: Settlers from Great Britain and Ireland
People from New Zealand
Chinese people who arrived during the gold rush
explanation_en: The early settlement section says Chinese people arriving at the time of the gold rush were the first large group of migrants not from Europe.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: What happened to Australia's population in the ten years after gold was discovered?
options_en: It stayed about the same
It fell as people left for the goldfields overseas
It more than doubled

guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: Why did people from all around the world travel to New South Wales and Victoria in the 1850s?
options_en: To try to make their fortunes from gold
To help build the new national capital
To take seats in the first federal parliament
explanation_en: The early settlement section says people came from all around the world to these colonies hoping to make their fortunes after gold was discovered.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement

stem_en: Where did the wealth that built many of Victoria's fine buildings come from?
options_en: Wool exports to Great Britain
The gold rush of the 1850s
Tourism to the Melbourne Cricket Ground
explanation_en: The section on the states says many fine buildings in Victoria were built from the wealth created by the gold rush of the 1850s.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which of these capital cities is the capital of a state, not of a territory?
options_en: Darwin
Canberra
Adelaide
explanation_en: The states and territories section lists Adelaide as the capital of South Australia, while Darwin and Canberra are the capitals of the two mainland territories.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Which pair correctly matches a state with its capital city?
options_en: Queensland — Sydney
Western Australia — Perth
Victoria — Hobart
explanation_en: The states and territories section pairs Western Australia with Perth; Sydney is the capital of New South Wales and Hobart of Tasmania.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Which of these icons is in Queensland rather than Western Australia?
options_en: The Great Barrier Reef
The Kimberley region
Margaret River
explanation_en: The section on the states places the Great Barrier Reef along Queensland's eastern coast, while the Kimberley and Margaret River are Western Australian icons.
guideRef: Part 1 — The states

stem_en: Which of these is NOT one of Australia's six states?
options_en: South Australia
Tasmania
The Australian Capital Territory
explanation_en: The states and territories section lists six states and two mainland territories; the Australian Capital Territory is a territory.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories

stem_en: Australia Day is celebrated each year on
options_en: 25 April
26 January
11 November
explanation_en: Part 1 says Australia Day is celebrated on 26 January each year.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: In which parts of Australia is Australia Day a public holiday?
options_en: New South Wales and Victoria only
Every state and territory
The Australian Capital Territory only
explanation_en: Part 1 says Australia Day is a public holiday in every state and territory in Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: Australia Day marks the anniversary of
options_en: the Federation of the colonies in 1901
the First Fleet's arrival in 1788
the Anzac landing at Gallipoli in 1915
explanation_en: The booklet says Australia Day is the anniversary of the arrival of the First Fleet from Great Britain in 1788.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: What do communities do on Australia Day?
options_en: Cast their votes in national, state and local elections
Close every court, school and parliament for the whole week
Reflect on the nation's history and shared achievements
explanation_en: Part 1 says that on Australia Day communities reflect on Australia's history and the people who contributed to shared achievements.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: The biggest annual public holiday in Australia is
options_en: Australia Day
Christmas Day
Easter Sunday
explanation_en: The booklet describes Australia Day as the biggest annual public holiday in Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: Which events are held across Australia on Australia Day?
options_en: Federal and state budget speeches
Special citizenship ceremonies
Openings of the national parliament
explanation_en: The booklet says Australia Day is marked by events across Australia, including special citizenship ceremonies.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: Who announces the Australian of the Year Awards?
options_en: The Governor-General
The Chief Justice
The Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra during Australia Day celebrations.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day

stem_en: On which date is Anzac Day held?
options_en: 25 April
26 January
11 November
explanation_en: Part 1 says Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April each year.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: The word 'Anzac' comes from the
options_en: Australian National Zone Army Command
Australia New Zealand Allied Council
Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
explanation_en: The booklet explains that Anzac Day is named after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Gallipoli in which country?
options_en: France
Germany
Türkiye
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye on 25 April 1915.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: The landing at Gallipoli took place during
options_en: World War I
the Vietnam War
the Korean War
explanation_en: The booklet says the Anzacs landed at Gallipoli during World War I, on 25 April 1915.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: Which best describes Anzac Day?
options_en: A solemn day of remembrance
A celebration of Federation
A festival marking the end of summer
explanation_en: The booklet describes Anzac Day as a solemn day when Australians remember the sacrifice of those who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: Besides remembering those who died, on Anzac Day Australians also honour
options_en: the commitment and courage of those who have served
the achievements of Australia's national sporting teams
the explorers who first mapped the Australian coastline
explanation_en: The booklet says that on Anzac Day we also honour the courage and commitment of all servicemen and women and reflect on the meanings of war.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: Which day is a time of remembrance rather than celebration?
options_en: Anzac Day
Australia Day
New Year's Day
explanation_en: Part 1 contrasts Australia Day, a celebration, with Anzac Day, a solemn day of remembrance for those who served and died.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: The official flag of the nation is
options_en: the flag of the United Kingdom
the Australian National Flag
the Australian Aboriginal Flag
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Australian National Flag is the official flag of the nation.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Besides the Australian National Flag, which two other flags are officially recognised in Australia?
options_en: The flags of New Zealand and the United Kingdom
The flags of the Olympic and Commonwealth Games
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags
explanation_en: The booklet says the Australian Aboriginal Flag and the Torres Strait Islander Flag are officially recognised and may be flown in the community.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Does each state and territory have its own flag?
options_en: No, only the six states have flags
Yes, each has its own flag
No, only the national flag is used
explanation_en: Part 1 says each state and territory also has its own flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which three colours appear on the Australian National Flag?
options_en: Blue, white and red
Green, gold and white
Black, red and yellow
explanation_en: The booklet says the Australian National Flag is blue, white and red.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which flag is in the top left corner of the Australian National Flag?
options_en: The Union Jack
The Southern Cross
The Commonwealth Star
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Union Jack, the flag of the United Kingdom, is in the top left corner of the national flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the national flag, the Union Jack represents
options_en: the history of British settlement
the six states and the territories
the stars of the southern sky
explanation_en: The booklet says the Union Jack represents Australia's history of British settlement and the laws and institutions inherited as a result.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Where is the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag?
options_en: In the top right corner
In the centre of the flag
Under the Union Jack
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Commonwealth Star sits under the Union Jack.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: How many points does the Commonwealth Star have?
options_en: Seven
Six
Eight
explanation_en: The booklet says the Commonwealth Star has seven points.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Six points of the Commonwealth Star stand for the states. What does the seventh point represent?
options_en: The Commonwealth Government
The United Kingdom
The territories
explanation_en: Part 1 explains that each point represents one of the six states, and one point represents the territories.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Australian National Flag, what is the Southern Cross?
options_en: A symbol of the British monarchy
A map of the six states and two territories
A group of stars seen in the southern sky
explanation_en: The booklet says the Southern Cross is a group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which flag is black, red and yellow?
options_en: The Australian Aboriginal Flag
The Torres Strait Islander Flag
The Australian National Flag
explanation_en: The booklet says the Australian Aboriginal Flag is black, red and yellow.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, the black top half represents
options_en: the night sky over the Australian continent
the Aboriginal peoples of Australia
the deep waters of the ocean
explanation_en: Part 1 says the top half of the Aboriginal Flag is black and represents the Aboriginal peoples of Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, the red bottom half represents
options_en: the sun
the earth
the night sky
explanation_en: The booklet says the red bottom half represents the earth, which has ceremonial significance.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: The yellow circle on the Australian Aboriginal Flag represents
options_en: the sun
the moon
a campfire
explanation_en: Part 1 says the yellow circle on the Aboriginal Flag represents the sun.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: A flag shows the sun as a yellow circle. Which flag is it?
options_en: The Torres Strait Islander Flag
The Australian National Flag
The Australian Aboriginal Flag
explanation_en: The booklet says the yellow circle on the Australian Aboriginal Flag represents the sun.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which flag is green, blue, black and white?
options_en: The Australian Aboriginal Flag
The Torres Strait Islander Flag
The Australian National Flag
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Torres Strait Islander Flag is green, blue, black and white.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, the green stripes represent
options_en: the sea
the people
the land
explanation_en: The booklet says the green stripes on the Torres Strait Islander Flag represent the land.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: The blue panel in the centre of the Torres Strait Islander Flag represents
options_en: the sea
the sky
the land
explanation_en: Part 1 says the blue panel in the centre of the Torres Strait Islander Flag represents the sea.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: What do the black lines on the Torres Strait Islander Flag stand for?
options_en: the night and the darkness of the sea
the earth, which has ceremonial significance
the Torres Strait Islander people
explanation_en: The booklet says the black lines on the Torres Strait Islander Flag represent the Torres Strait Islander people.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, what does the white dancer's headdress stand for?
options_en: The Australian Government
The Royal Australian Navy's ships
All Torres Strait Islanders
explanation_en: Part 1 says the white dancer's headdress in the centre of the flag is a symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: On the Torres Strait Islander Flag, the points of the white star represent
options_en: the six states of the Commonwealth
the main languages spoken on the islands
the island groups in the Torres Strait
explanation_en: The booklet says the points of the white star represent the island groups in the Torres Strait.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which flag has a star whose points represent island groups?
options_en: The Australian National Flag
The Torres Strait Islander Flag
The Australian Aboriginal Flag
explanation_en: Part 1 says the points of the white star on the Torres Strait Islander Flag represent the island groups, while the Commonwealth Star on the national flag represents the states and territories.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which of these is the Commonwealth of Australia's official symbol?
options_en: the Southern Cross constellation
the golden wattle flower
the Commonwealth Coat of Arms
explanation_en: Part 1 says the Commonwealth Coat of Arms is the official symbol of the Commonwealth of Australia and represents national unity.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: What does the Commonwealth Coat of Arms identify?
options_en: The property of each of the state governments
The authority and property of the Commonwealth
The personal property of the monarch and royal family
explanation_en: The booklet says the Coat of Arms identifies the authority and property of the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: What does the central shield of the Coat of Arms stand for?
options_en: The Australian Defence Force
The six states and federation
The two mainland territories only
explanation_en: Part 1 says the shield in the centre of the Coat of Arms represents the six states and federation.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which two native animals support the shield on the Coat of Arms?
options_en: A kangaroo and an emu
A koala and a platypus
A wombat and a kookaburra
explanation_en: The booklet says a kangaroo and an emu, both native Australian animals, support the shield on each side.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which element appears on both the Australian National Flag and the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
options_en: The Union Jack
The Southern Cross constellation
The Commonwealth Star
explanation_en: The booklet places the Commonwealth Star under the Union Jack on the national flag and above the shield on the Coat of Arms.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: The background of the Commonwealth Coat of Arms is
options_en: the Southern Cross
the golden wattle
the Union Jack
explanation_en: Part 1 says the background of the Coat of Arms is the golden wattle, Australia's national flower.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which plant is Australia's national flower?
options_en: the red waratah
the golden wattle
the Sturt's desert pea
explanation_en: The booklet says Australia's national flower is the golden wattle.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Besides the national golden wattle, what does each state and territory have?
options_en: Its own floral emblem
Its own national gemstone
Its own national anthem
explanation_en: The booklet says each of the states and territories also has its own floral emblem.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Australia's national colours are
options_en: blue and white
green and gold
red and black
explanation_en: Part 1 says Australia's national colours are green and gold.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Why are green and gold Australia's national colours?
options_en: They are the colours of the Union Jack
They are the colours of the golden wattle
They are the colours of the Southern Cross
explanation_en: The booklet explains that green and gold are the colours of the golden wattle, the national flower.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Australia's national gemstone is
options_en: the opal
the sapphire
the diamond
explanation_en: The booklet says the opal is Australia's national gemstone.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Australia's national anthem is
options_en: 'Waltzing Matilda'
'Advance Australia Fair'
'I Still Call Australia Home'
explanation_en: The booklet says 'Advance Australia Fair' is Australia's national anthem.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's national anthem

stem_en: The national anthem is sung at
options_en: the opening of every court case
the start of every school day, as required by law
citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events
explanation_en: Part 1 says the anthem is sung on occasions of national importance, including citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's national anthem

stem_en: Which is the first line of 'Advance Australia Fair'?
options_en: Australians all let us rejoice
Our home is girt by sea
Beneath our radiant Southern Cross
explanation_en: The booklet prints the anthem, which opens with the line 'Australians all let us rejoice, for we are one and free'.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's national anthem

stem_en: According to Aboriginal legend, what created the colours of the opal?
options_en: A rainbow touching the earth
Sunlight shining on the sea
Fire sweeping across the desert
explanation_en: The symbols section recounts the Aboriginal legend that a rainbow touched the earth and created the colours of the opal, Australia's national gemstone.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: What colours do Australia's national sports teams usually wear?
options_en: Navy blue and silver
Green and gold
Maroon and white
explanation_en: The symbols section says the uniforms of Australia's national sports teams are usually green and gold, the national colours.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: On which part of the Australian National Flag is the Southern Cross?
options_en: Beneath the Union Jack
In the top left corner
On the right-hand side
explanation_en: The flags section describes the Southern Cross as the group of stars on the right of the national flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: In which season does the golden wattle produce its many golden yellow flowers?
options_en: Spring
Autumn
Winter
explanation_en: The symbols section describes the golden wattle as a small tree with bright green leaves and many golden yellow flowers in spring.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: In which part of Australia does the golden wattle mainly grow?
options_en: The tropical far north
The deserts of Western Australia
South-eastern Australia
explanation_en: The symbols section says the golden wattle grows mainly in south-eastern Australia.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which of these is an official national symbol rather than a flag?
options_en: The Torres Strait Islander Flag
The Commonwealth Coat of Arms
The Australian Aboriginal Flag
explanation_en: The symbols section describes the Commonwealth Coat of Arms as the official symbol of the Commonwealth of Australia; the other two are officially recognised flags.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which of these belongs to the Australian National Flag rather than the Australian Aboriginal Flag?
options_en: A yellow circle
The Southern Cross
A black upper half
explanation_en: The flags section places the Southern Cross on the national flag, while the black upper half and yellow circle are features of the Australian Aboriginal Flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which of these appears on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms but not on the Australian National Flag?
options_en: A kangaroo and an emu
The Commonwealth Star
The Union Jack
explanation_en: The symbols section says a kangaroo and an emu support the shield of the Coat of Arms; the Commonwealth Star appears on both, and the Union Jack only on the flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols

stem_en: Which of these is NOT a colour of the Torres Strait Islander Flag?
options_en: Green
Red
Blue
explanation_en: The flags section describes the Torres Strait Islander Flag as green, blue, black and white; red belongs to the Australian Aboriginal Flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

stem_en: Which of these describes Anzac Day rather than Australia Day?
options_en: The biggest annual public holiday in Australia
The day the Australian of the Year Awards are announced
A solemn day remembering those who served and died in wars
explanation_en: The important days section describes Anzac Day as a solemn day of remembrance, while the Australian of the Year Awards and the biggest public holiday belong to Australia Day.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

stem_en: Besides sharing Australia's democratic beliefs, what do new citizens pledge at the ceremony?
options_en: To join an Australian political party
To respect Australia's rights and liberties
To follow Australia's official religion
explanation_en: Part 2 opens by saying that at the citizenship ceremony you pledge to share Australia's democratic beliefs and respect its rights and liberties.
guideRef: Part 2 — Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties

stem_en: What kind of system of government does Australia have?
options_en: A parliamentary democracy
A monarchy with absolute power
A government run by the military
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australia's system of government is a parliamentary democracy.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, the power of the government comes from
options_en: the King acting alone
the Australian people
the judges of the High Court
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that the power of the government comes from the Australian people, because citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: How do Australian citizens give the government its power?
options_en: By paying a yearly membership fee to the parliament
By voting for people to represent them in parliament
By serving a period of time in the Australian Defence Force
explanation_en: The booklet says power comes from the people because Australian citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: In a parliamentary democracy, members of parliament are chosen by
options_en: citizens voting in elections
the Governor-General acting alone
the judges of the courts
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australian citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Members of parliament are held accountable to the people for their decisions through
options_en: elections
the courts
the police
explanation_en: Part 2 says representatives in parliament must answer to the people, through elections, for the decisions they make.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Voters are unhappy with the decisions their representatives have made. How do they hold them to account?
options_en: By voting at the next election
By asking the police to remove them
By writing to the King for a ruling
explanation_en: The booklet explains that representatives answer to the people through elections for the decisions they make.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Under Australian law, all Australians are
options_en: ranked by wealth
equal
ranked by birthplace
explanation_en: Part 2 states that all Australians are equal under the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A friend says wealthy people are treated better by Australian courts. In Australia's legal system,
options_en: wealthier people have more legal rights
only citizens are equal under the law
all Australians are equal under the law
explanation_en: Part 2 says all Australians are equal under the law, which is the basis of the Rule of Law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: The Rule of Law means that
options_en: the police may write their own laws
religious leaders decide what is legal
nobody is above the law
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that the Rule of Law means no person, group or religious rule is above the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A business owner says the law does not apply to someone as wealthy as him. Which Australian belief does this go against?
options_en: The Rule of Law
Freedom of association
Equality of opportunity
explanation_en: The Rule of Law, described in Part 2, means no person or group is above the law, however wealthy or powerful.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A religious leader tells followers that religious rules replace Australian law. Is this correct?
options_en: Yes, religious leaders are above the law
Yes, but only for members of that religion
No, no religious rule is above the law
explanation_en: Part 2 says the Rule of Law means no person, group or religious rule is above the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Who must obey Australia's laws?
options_en: Only people who were not born in Australia
Everyone, including people in positions of power
Only people who do not hold a position in government
explanation_en: Part 2 says everyone, including people who hold positions of power in the community, must obey Australia's laws.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A police officer breaks a road rule. In Australia, the officer
options_en: is above the law while on duty
must obey the law like everyone else
answers only to other police officers
explanation_en: The booklet lists the police among those who must obey Australia's laws, along with government, community and religious leaders and business people.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which statement about leaders in Australia is correct?
options_en: Government leaders are exempt from the law
Government and religious leaders must obey the law
Religious leaders may ignore laws they disagree with
explanation_en: Part 2 says government, community and religious leaders, as well as business people and the police, must all obey Australia's laws.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: What kind of country are Australians proud to live in?
options_en: Peaceful, with a stable system of government
Constantly changing its government through force
Governed without holding any elections
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians are proud to live in a peaceful country with a stable system of government.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: How do Australians believe change in society should come about?
options_en: Through discussion and the democratic process
Through threats and intimidation of opponents
Through orders issued by religious leaders
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians believe change should occur through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: You want a law changed. Which approach reflects Australian democratic beliefs?
options_en: Threatening members of parliament until they agree
Peaceful persuasion through the democratic process
Damaging public property to force the issue
explanation_en: The booklet says change should come through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process, and it rejects violence.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: In Australia, using violence to change someone's mind or to change the law is
options_en: accepted if the cause is just
accepted during election campaigns
rejected
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Someone disagrees with a new law and hits a politician to make a point. According to Australian values, this is
options_en: never acceptable
acceptable if the law is unfair
acceptable once in each election
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which statement reflects Australian democratic beliefs?
options_en: Violence is acceptable as a way to change an unfair law
Violence is rejected as a way to change the law
Violence is acceptable if many people agree
explanation_en: The booklet says Australians reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Australia's democratic system rests on which principle about individuals?
options_en: Everyone must follow the religion of the majority
Rights are gained by owning property or wealth
Everyone has rights and equality under the law
explanation_en: Part 2 says the democratic system is based on the principle that every individual, regardless of background, has rights and equality under Australian law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: In Australia, people are expected to treat one another with
options_en: suspicion and caution
dignity and respect
distance and formality
explanation_en: Part 2 says all Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect, regardless of their background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A new colleague comes from a different country and culture. Australians are expected to
options_en: ask them to give up their own culture
avoid working alongside them
treat them with dignity and respect
explanation_en: The booklet says Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect regardless of race, country of origin or culture.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which best reflects respect for all individuals regardless of background?
options_en: Respecting only people who share your own beliefs
Treating a person fairly whatever their religion or politics
Treating people differently depending on how wealthy they are
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect regardless of religion, politics, wealth and other differences.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Australian laws protect people from being treated differently because of which characteristics?
options_en: Income level, postcode or occupation
Favourite sport or hobbies
Gender, race, disability or age
explanation_en: Part 2 says a number of laws ensure a person is not treated differently because of their gender, race, disability or age.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: Which of these is covered by Australia's laws against unequal treatment?
options_en: A person's level of income
A person's postcode
A person's disability
explanation_en: The booklet says laws ensure people are not treated differently because of their gender, race, disability or age.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: In Australia, men and women
options_en: have equal rights
have different legal rights
vote in separate elections
explanation_en: Part 2 says men and women have equal rights in Australia.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: A woman wants to stand for election to parliament. In Australia she
options_en: needs permission from a male relative
cannot stand because of her gender
has the same right to do so as a man
explanation_en: The booklet says men and women have equal rights in Australia and that discrimination because of gender is against the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: An employer says a job is open only to men because women should not work. In Australia, this
options_en: is against the law
is allowed if the employer owns the business
is allowed for jobs that pay a high salary
explanation_en: Part 2 says it is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: Which statement about gender in Australia is correct?
options_en: Employers may pay women less because of their gender
Only men are allowed to hold senior positions of power in Australia
Discriminating against someone because of their gender is illegal
explanation_en: The booklet's section on gender equality says it is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: What everyday phrase do Australians use for equal opportunity?
options_en: A 'fair go'
A 'free ride'
A 'class system'
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australians value equal opportunity in society, often called a 'fair go'.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: A 'fair go' means what someone achieves in life should result from
options_en: their family's wealth
their talents, work and effort
the social class they were born into
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that a fair go means what someone achieves should result from their talents, work and effort rather than their wealth or background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: Two people apply for the same job. According to the idea of a 'fair go', who should get it?
options_en: The person who comes from the wealthier family
The person whose parents had the higher standing in society
The person with the better talents and effort for the job
explanation_en: The booklet says a fair go means success should come from talents, work and effort, not wealth or background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: A child from a poor family works hard and becomes a doctor. This is an example of
options_en: a class distinction
a 'fair go'
the Rule of Law
explanation_en: Part 2 describes a fair go as achievement resulting from talent, work and effort rather than wealth or background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: Equality of opportunity is meant to ensure that Australian society has
options_en: a strict and formal class system
a ruling class based on birth
no formal class distinctions
explanation_en: Part 2 says equal opportunity is meant to ensure there are no formal class distinctions in Australian society.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: In Australia, 'democracy' means
options_en: rule by a hereditary monarch without any elections
rule by the people through elected representatives
rule by military leaders chosen by the army
explanation_en: The glossary defines democracy as government by the people through elected representatives.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A 'parliamentary democracy' is a system of government based on
options_en: the King appointing representatives to parliament for life
the courts selecting representatives to sit in parliament
citizens regularly electing representatives to parliament
explanation_en: The glossary defines parliamentary democracy as a system based on the regular election of representatives to parliament by the citizens.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In Australia, the Rule of Law binds
options_en: all people, including the Prime Minister
only ordinary citizens, not the government
only people who were born in Australia
explanation_en: The glossary says the Rule of Law means all people, including citizens and the government, are bound by the law, even the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A Prime Minister is found to have broken a law. Under the Rule of Law, the Prime Minister
options_en: must face the law like anyone else
is excused because of the office they hold
can be judged only by the parliament
explanation_en: The glossary entry for the Rule of Law says all people, including the government and even the Prime Minister, are bound by the law.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In Australia, 'equality' means
options_en: having greater wealth
the same in status
being older than others
explanation_en: The glossary defines equality as being the same in status.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: The Australian idea of a 'fair go' is
options_en: an equal opportunity for everyone to succeed in life
the same income for every person living in Australia
the same amount of property for every Australian family
explanation_en: The glossary says a fair go means everyone, regardless of background, is given an equal opportunity to achieve success in life.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In Australian society, 'respect' means
options_en: agreeing with everything another person says
obeying another person's instructions without question
showing consideration for a person or their decision
explanation_en: The glossary defines respect as showing consideration for someone as a person, or for a decision they have made.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Australia's 'liberties' are freedom of
options_en: speech, expression, religion and association
driving, fishing, hunting and camping
taking any job without needing any qualifications
explanation_en: The glossary defines liberties as personal freedom and independence: freedom of speech, expression, religion and association.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which of these is one of Australia's liberties?
options_en: Compulsory voting in elections
Paying income tax
Freedom of religion
explanation_en: The glossary lists freedom of speech, expression, religion and association as Australia's liberties.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: What do Australians reject as a way of changing a person's mind or changing the law?
options_en: Public debate
Violence
Voting at elections
explanation_en: The 'living peacefully' belief in the democratic beliefs section says Australians reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or the law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: What is a system of government based on regularly electing representatives to parliament called?
options_en: A constitutional monarchy
A federation of states
A parliamentary democracy
explanation_en: The glossary defines a parliamentary democracy as a system of government based on the regular election of representatives to parliament by the citizens.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which statement about who must obey Australia's laws is correct?
options_en: Everyone, including religious leaders and the police
Everyone except people who hold positions of power
Only people who are not yet Australian citizens
explanation_en: The Rule of Law belief says everyone must obey the law, and the democratic beliefs section specifically names government, community and religious leaders, business people and the police.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which of these situations reflects the Rule of Law?
options_en: Senior police officers are exempt from traffic laws
A judge is held to the same laws as any other person
Business leaders can pay to avoid prosecution
explanation_en: The democratic beliefs section says no person, group or religious rule is above the law, so a judge is bound by the law like everyone else.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which of these is one of Australia's democratic beliefs rather than one of its equalities?
options_en: Gender equality
A 'fair go'
Living peacefully
explanation_en: Part 2 lists living peacefully among the democratic beliefs, while gender equality and the 'fair go' appear under 'Our equalities'.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A manager pays a 55-year-old worker less than her younger colleagues purely because of her age. In Australia, this
options_en: is allowed if the business is small
is a private matter between employer and worker
goes against laws that stop different treatment because of age
explanation_en: The equalities section says Australian laws ensure a person is not treated differently because of their gender, race, disability or age.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: At an election, voters remove a politician whose decisions they disagreed with. Which democratic belief does this show?
options_en: Representatives answer to the people through elections
The Rule of Law
Freedom of religion
explanation_en: The parliamentary democracy belief says representatives in parliament must answer to the people, through elections, for the decisions they make.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which of these is NOT one of Australia's four democratic beliefs?
options_en: Loyalty to the King
Living peacefully
Respect for all individuals regardless of background
explanation_en: The democratic beliefs section lists parliamentary democracy, the Rule of Law, living peacefully and respect for all individuals; loyalty to the King is not among them.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: A landlord says only people born in Australia may apply to rent his flat. Which democratic belief does this go against?
options_en: Parliamentary democracy
Respect for all individuals regardless of background
Living peacefully
explanation_en: The democratic beliefs section says every individual, regardless of background such as country of origin, has rights and equality under Australian law and deserves dignity and respect.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs

stem_en: Which of these is an example of the 'fair go' principle?
options_en: Promotion based on skill and effort
Jobs reserved for people from wealthy families
Pay set according to a person's country of origin
explanation_en: The equalities section says a 'fair go' means what someone achieves should come from their talents, work and effort rather than their wealth or background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities

stem_en: In Australia, freedom of speech is
options_en: a privilege for citizens only
a rule created by the courts
a core Australian value
explanation_en: Part 2 says freedom of speech is a core Australian value and underpins the democratic system.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which freedom underpins Australia's democratic system?
options_en: Freedom of speech
Freedom from taxation
Freedom to ignore laws
explanation_en: Part 2 says freedom of speech is a core Australian value and underpins Australia's democratic system.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which of these is part of freedom of speech in Australia?
options_en: Saying anything at all without having to obey the law
Writing down what you think and discussing it with others
Stopping other people from sharing their opinions
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that freedom of speech means people can say and write what they think and discuss their ideas with others.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Two neighbours discuss their different political ideas over the fence. In Australia this is
