options_en: an example of freedom of speech
against the law in public places
allowed only during election campaigns
explanation_en: The booklet says freedom of speech means people can say what they think and discuss their ideas with others.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: In Australia, people are allowed to criticise the government
options_en: only if they belong to a political party
only in private conversations at home
as long as they obey the law
explanation_en: Part 2 says people can criticise the government, protest peacefully and campaign to change laws, so long as they obey Australian laws.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: A group wants to protest peacefully against a government decision. In Australia they
options_en: are free to do so while obeying the law
must first get permission from the Prime Minister
are not permitted to protest against the government
explanation_en: The booklet gives protesting peacefully against government decisions as an example of freedom of speech, provided the law is obeyed.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Campaigning to change an Australian law is
options_en: allowed, so long as the law is obeyed
a crime unless parliament gives permission
allowed only for members of parliament
explanation_en: Part 2 says people can campaign to change laws as part of freedom of speech, so long as they obey Australian laws.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which activity is allowed under freedom of speech in Australia?
options_en: Criticising the government
Threatening a politician
Damaging a government office
explanation_en: The booklet says people can criticise the government, but the laws of Australia must be obeyed at all times.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which of these is a way of exercising freedom of expression?
options_en: Violence and threats of violence
Damaging other people's property
Art, film, music and literature
explanation_en: Part 2 says freedom of expression means people can express their views, including through art, film, music and literature.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: A musician writes a song criticising a government policy. In Australia this is
options_en: against the law and can be punished
allowed only with government approval
an example of freedom of expression
explanation_en: The booklet says freedom of expression includes expressing views through art, film, music and literature.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which freedom covers expressing views through art and film?
options_en: Freedom of association
Freedom of religion
Freedom of expression
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that freedom of expression means people can express their views through art, film, music and literature.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: In Australia, people are free to meet for social or political discussion
options_en: only in their own private homes
in public or private places
only inside parliament buildings
explanation_en: Part 2 says people are free to meet in public or private places for social or political discussion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: A family invites their neighbours home to discuss a political issue. In Australia this is
options_en: allowed; people may meet in private or public places for this
allowed only if the local council is told in advance
not allowed; political discussion belongs in parliament
explanation_en: The booklet says people are free to meet in public or private places for social or political discussion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Even while exercising freedom of speech, people in Australia must
options_en: register their views with the government
agree with the majority opinion
obey the law at all times
explanation_en: Part 2 says that at all times, even while engaging in freedom of speech and expression, the laws of Australia must be obeyed.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: A person claims freedom of speech lets them break any law while protesting. Is this correct?
options_en: Yes, protests are exempt from the law
No, the law must be obeyed at all times
Yes, if the protest is about the government
explanation_en: The booklet is clear that even while engaging in freedom of speech and expression, Australian laws must be obeyed at all times.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which statement about freedom of speech is correct?
options_en: We must also respect other people's freedom of speech
Only our own freedom of speech needs to be respected
Freedom of speech applies only to elected politicians
explanation_en: Part 2 says we must also respect other people's freedom of speech and freedom of expression.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Someone on the radio expresses a view you strongly disagree with. According to Australian values, you should
options_en: demand that the radio station be shut down immediately
threaten the speaker until they stop
respect their freedom to express their view
explanation_en: The booklet says we must respect other people's freedom of speech and freedom of expression.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which best shows respect for another person's freedom of expression?
options_en: Demanding that the artwork be removed from display
Letting an artist display work you dislike
Damaging the artwork in protest
explanation_en: Part 2 says we must respect other people's freedom of speech and expression, which includes expression through art.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: What does freedom of association allow people to do?
options_en: Travel to any country without needing a passport
Form and join groups with shared goals
Choose which laws they will obey
explanation_en: Part 2 defines freedom of association as the right to form and join associations to pursue common goals.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Under freedom of association, people in Australia are free to join
options_en: only organisations approved by the government
only religious groups and churches
any legal organisation, such as a trade union
explanation_en: The booklet says people are free to join any legal organisation, such as a political party, trade union, or religious, cultural or social group.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Which is an example of freedom of association?
options_en: Refusing to pay income tax
Joining a political party
Ignoring a court order
explanation_en: Part 2 gives joining a political party, trade union, or religious, cultural or social group as examples of freedom of association.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: A worker wants to join a trade union. In Australia
options_en: they need their employer's permission
they are free to join
trade union membership is illegal
explanation_en: The booklet lists trade unions among the legal organisations people are free to join.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Which of these is covered by freedom of association rather than freedom of speech?
options_en: Joining a trade union
Writing a letter criticising the government
Making a film about politics
explanation_en: Part 2 says freedom of association is the right to form and join associations, such as a trade union, while criticising the government and making films fall under freedom of speech and expression.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Can a person in Australia be forced to join an organisation?
options_en: Yes, if their employer requires it
No, people can decide not to join
Yes, if the government requires it
explanation_en: Part 2 says people can decide not to join an organisation and cannot be forced into doing so.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: A neighbour insists you must join their political party. In Australia
options_en: you must join if a neighbour asks you to
you must join at least one political party
nobody can force you to join
explanation_en: The booklet says people can decide not to join an organisation and cannot be forced into doing so.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Which statement about joining organisations in Australia is correct?
options_en: Joining is a free choice; nobody can be forced
Everyone must join a trade union
Everyone must join at least one political party
explanation_en: Part 2 says people are free to join any legal organisation and can also decide not to join.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Australians can gather to protest against a government action, but the gathering must
options_en: be approved in advance by the Prime Minister
be peaceful and cause no injury or damage
take place only in the national capital, Canberra
explanation_en: Part 2 says protest gatherings must be peaceful and must not injure any person or damage property.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: During a protest, some people start damaging shops. In Australia, this is
options_en: allowed as part of freedom of association
against the law, even during a protest
allowed when protesting a government decision
explanation_en: The booklet says gatherings must be peaceful and must not injure any person or damage property, because the law must be obeyed at all times.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Australia's heritage is
options_en: Buddhist and Taoist
Hindu and Sikh
Judaeo-Christian
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australia has a Judaeo-Christian heritage, and many Australians describe themselves as Christians.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: In Australia there are people from
options_en: only Christian churches
all the large religions
only one official religion
explanation_en: The booklet says that although many Australians describe themselves as Christians, there are people in Australia from all the large religions.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which Christian days are public holidays in Australia?
options_en: Christmas Day only, and no other Christian day
No Christian days are public holidays in Australia
Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australia has public holidays on Christian days such as Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: How do the government and the law treat citizens of different religions?
options_en: Equally, whatever their beliefs
More favourably if they are Christian
More favourably if they have no religion
explanation_en: Part 2 says the government and the law treat all citizens equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A person who follows a minority religion goes to court. Under Australian law they are
options_en: treated less favourably than Christians
treated equally, whatever their religion
required to change their religion beforehand
explanation_en: The booklet says the government and the law treat all citizens equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: What does it mean that Australia's government is secular?
options_en: It is run by leaders of the largest churches
It chooses one official religion for everyone
It operates separately from religious bodies
explanation_en: Part 2 says the government in Australia is secular, meaning it operates separately from churches or other religious entities.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which word describes a government that operates separately from religion?
options_en: Federal
Parliamentary
Secular
explanation_en: The booklet uses the word secular to describe a government that operates separately from churches or other religious entities.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which statement about religion in Australia is correct?
options_en: Christianity is Australia's official religion
Australia has no official national religion
Every Australian must register a religion
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australia has no official national religion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which statement about religious choice in Australia is correct?
options_en: People may follow only the Christian faith and its churches
People may follow any religion, or none at all
People may follow only the religion of their parents
explanation_en: Part 2 says people in Australia are free to follow any religion they choose, and may also choose not to follow a religion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Your friend decides not to follow any religion. In Australia this is
options_en: their free choice
against the law
allowed only for non-citizens
explanation_en: The booklet says people may choose not to follow a religion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A migrant wants to keep practising the religion of their home country in Australia. Can they?
options_en: Yes, they may follow any religion they choose
No, they must adopt Australia's majority religion
Only if that religion is Christian
explanation_en: Part 2 says people in Australia are free to follow any religion they choose.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Even while engaging in religious practices, people in Australia must
options_en: obey Australian law
register with a church
pay a religious tax
explanation_en: Part 2 says that at all times, even while engaging in religious practices, the laws of Australia must be obeyed.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: If an Australian law conflicts with a religious practice, which prevails?
options_en: The religious practice
Whichever the person chooses
Australian law
explanation_en: Part 2 says that where there is a conflict between an Australian law and a religious practice, Australian law prevails.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A religious practice conflicts with an Australian law. A person following that religion
options_en: may ignore the Australian law
may choose which one to follow
must obey the Australian law
explanation_en: The booklet says Australian law prevails where it conflicts with a religious practice.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: The word 'secular' means
options_en: belonging to one church
separate from religion
governed by religious law
explanation_en: The glossary defines secular as separate from religion.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In a secular society there is
options_en: no official religion
one compulsory religion
a religious court above parliament
explanation_en: The glossary says that in a secular society there is no official religion.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: The word 'liberty' means
options_en: personal freedom and independence
obedience to those in authority
ownership of land, wealth and property
explanation_en: The glossary defines liberty as personal freedom and independence.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Public holidays such as Christmas Day and Good Friday come from which religious tradition?
options_en: Christian
Buddhist
Hindu
explanation_en: The freedom of religion section notes that Australia has public holidays on Christian days such as Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which freedom is the right to form and join associations to pursue common goals?
options_en: Freedom of expression
Freedom of association
Freedom of religion
explanation_en: The freedom of association section defines it as the right to form and join associations to pursue common goals.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: How many Australians call themselves Christians?
options_en: Very few Australians
Every Australian without exception
Many Australians
explanation_en: The freedom of religion section says many Australians describe themselves as Christians, while people from all the large religions live in Australia.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Deciding to follow no religion at all is an example of which freedom?
options_en: Freedom of religion
Freedom of association
Freedom of expression
explanation_en: The freedom of religion section says people in Australia are free to follow any religion they choose, and may also choose not to follow a religion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Which of these is an example of freedom of speech rather than freedom of religion?
options_en: Attending a weekly place of worship
Campaigning to change a law
Choosing not to follow any religion
explanation_en: The freedom of speech section gives campaigning to change laws as an example of free speech; following a religion, or none, belongs to freedom of religion.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Which of these stays within the limits Australia places on freedom of speech?
options_en: A protest that blocks a street and damages a shop front
Threatening a politician until she changes her vote
A peaceful march against a government decision
explanation_en: The freedom of speech section allows peaceful protest and campaigning against government decisions so long as Australian laws are obeyed at all times.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: Members of a cultural association want to start a new group to pursue a shared goal. In Australia they
options_en: need written approval from a religious authority first
must register the new group with a political party
are free to form and join such an association
explanation_en: The freedom of association section says people have the right to form and join associations to pursue common goals.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Your neighbour hangs a banner on her fence criticising a local council decision. In Australia this is
options_en: allowed, since people may criticise government decisions lawfully
illegal unless the council has approved the wording of the banner first
allowed only in the weeks before a local council election campaign
explanation_en: The freedom of speech section says people can say and write what they think and criticise the government, as long as they obey Australian laws.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

stem_en: During a lawful protest, a speaker urges the crowd to injure a police officer. In Australia, this
options_en: is protected as freedom of speech, whatever the speaker says
is not protected, because gatherings must be peaceful and injure no one
is acceptable as long as the officer is not actually hurt by anyone
explanation_en: The freedom of association section says protest gatherings must be peaceful and must not injure any person or damage property, and the laws of Australia must be obeyed.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: Which of these is NOT an example of a legal organisation people in Australia may freely join?
options_en: A trade union representing workers
A group that plans violent protests
A religious or cultural group
explanation_en: The freedom of association section lists political parties, trade unions and religious, cultural or social groups; violence and damage to property are never permitted.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association

stem_en: When you become an Australian citizen, you take on
options_en: additional responsibilities and privileges
fewer legal duties than permanent residents have
the right to ignore state laws
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that citizenship brings both new responsibilities (what you give Australia) and new privileges (what Australia gives you).
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

stem_en: Which of these is a responsibility of an Australian citizen?
options_en: Joining a political party
Serving on a jury if called
Owning a home somewhere in Australia
explanation_en: Part 2 lists four responsibilities: obey the law, vote, defend Australia if needed, and serve on a jury if called to do so.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

stem_en: Which of these is a privilege of Australian citizenship?
options_en: Paying a lower rate of income tax each year
Being excused from jury duty
Applying for an Australian passport
explanation_en: Part 2 lists applying for an Australian passport among the privileges that citizenship gives you.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

stem_en: As an Australian citizen you must
options_en: defend Australia should the need arise
attend a citizenship ceremony each year
join the Defence Force when you turn 18
explanation_en: Part 2 lists defending Australia should the need arise as one of the responsibilities of citizenship.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

stem_en: For Australian citizens, voting is
options_en: a privilege only
a responsibility only, never a privilege
both a responsibility and a privilege
explanation_en: Part 2 puts voting on both lists: it is something you must do and also something Australia gives you the right to do.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

stem_en: Who must obey the laws of Australia?
options_en: Only Australian citizens
Everyone in Australia, citizens or not
Only people who were born in Australia
explanation_en: Part 2 says all Australian citizens and all other people in Australia must obey Australian law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Why do our representatives in government make laws?
options_en: To decide which religion people follow
To limit who can become a citizen
To keep society orderly, free and safe
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that laws are made to maintain an orderly, free and safe society and to protect our rights.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Voting is a responsibility for Australian citizens aged
options_en: 16 years or over
18 years or over
21 years or over
explanation_en: Part 2 says voting is a responsibility, right and privilege for all Australian citizens aged 18 years or over.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: What does a referendum ask Australians to decide?
options_en: Which party forms government
Who should be the next Prime Minister
Whether to change the Constitution
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that a referendum is a vote to change the Australian Constitution.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: By voting, Australian citizens
options_en: get a say in the way Australia is governed
choose the judges of the High Court of Australia
are excused from paying tax
explanation_en: Part 2 says that by voting, citizens have a say in how Australia is governed and contribute to its future.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: In federal and state or territory elections, voting is
options_en: only for people born in Australia
compulsory
optional
explanation_en: Part 2 states that voting is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: In some states, voting may not be compulsory for
options_en: federal elections for the Senate
local government elections
state or territory elections
explanation_en: Part 2 notes that while voting is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections, it may not be compulsory in local government elections in some states.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Service in the Australian Defence Force is
options_en: voluntary
required before you can become a citizen
compulsory for all men
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that Defence Force service is voluntary, even though citizens have a responsibility to defend Australia should the need arise.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: If called to do so, Australian citizens aged 18 or over must
options_en: serve on a jury
work for the public service
stand for parliament
explanation_en: Part 2 says jury service, if requested, is a responsibility for Australian citizens aged 18 years or over.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: What does a jury do?
options_en: Writes new laws for parliament to pass
Listens to evidence and decides guilt
Chooses the judge for a trial
explanation_en: Part 2 describes a jury as people who listen to the evidence in a court case and decide if a person is guilty or not guilty.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: A jury is made up of
options_en: members of parliament
ordinary Australian men and women
lawyers chosen by the court to decide
explanation_en: Part 2 describes a jury as a group of ordinary Australian men and women.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Who may be called up for jury service?
options_en: Only people with legal training
Citizens who are on the electoral roll
Anyone who holds a valid Australian visa
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australian citizens who are on the electoral roll can be called to serve on a jury.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Jury service helps to make sure the court system is
options_en: controlled by the government
quick and cheap
open and fair
explanation_en: Part 2 says jury service helps to ensure that the court system is open and fair.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities

stem_en: Working at Services Australia or the ATO is an example of
options_en: a job in the Australian Public Service
a position on a local council
serving in the Australian Defence Force
explanation_en: Part 2 gives Services Australia and the Australian Taxation Office as examples of Australian Public Service employers that citizens can apply to.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: The Army, Navy and Air Force make up
options_en: the Australian Federal Police
the Australian Defence Force
the Australian Public Service
explanation_en: Part 2 says citizens can apply for a job in the Australian Defence Force, which is the Army, Navy and Air Force.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Who can seek election to an Australian parliament?
options_en: Only citizens who were born in Australia
Any permanent resident who has lived here five years
Citizens aged 18 or over who are not dual citizens
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australian citizens aged 18 or over who are not dual citizens can seek election at federal, state or territory level.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: A dual citizen aged 30 wants to stand for the Senate. Under Australian rules,
options_en: they may stand if they pay a special fee
dual citizens cannot seek election
they may stand only in a state election
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that only citizens who are not dual citizens can seek election to parliament at any level.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Serving in an Australian parliament is described as
options_en: an honour and a serious responsibility
a well-paid part-time job
a duty every Australian citizen must perform
explanation_en: Part 2 says it is an honour and a serious responsibility to serve in an Australian parliament.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Which document can an Australian citizen, but not a permanent resident, apply for?
options_en: A tax file number from the ATO
A driver licence
An Australian passport
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that applying for an Australian passport is a privilege of citizenship.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: An Australian citizen returning from an overseas trip
options_en: does not need a visa to re-enter
must apply for a visa first
must show a permanent residency card
explanation_en: Part 2 says a citizen who travels overseas is free to return to Australia without the need for a visa.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Becoming a citizen gives you the right to
options_en: live freely in Australia
vote in another country's elections
avoid paying income tax
explanation_en: Part 2 says that when you become a citizen you have the right to live freely in Australia.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Where can Australians overseas ask an Australian official for help?
options_en: At an embassy, high commission or consulate
At the nearest international airport's help desk
At any local police station
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that Australia has an embassy, high commission or consulate in many countries where citizens can ask for help.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: You are overseas when a natural disaster strikes. As an Australian citizen you can
options_en: demand a free flight home from the ATO
ignore the laws of that country
ask Australian officials for help
explanation_en: Part 2 says citizens overseas can ask Australian officials for help in times of need, including emergencies such as civil unrest and natural disasters.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Australian officials overseas can help a citizen who has lost their passport by
options_en: giving them a new tourist visa
paying for their hotel
issuing an emergency passport
explanation_en: Part 2 lists the issue of an emergency passport among the consular help available to Australian citizens overseas.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: When you are in another country as an Australian citizen, you must
options_en: register with the local council
follow only Australian laws
obey the laws of that country
explanation_en: Part 2 reminds citizens that when in another country they must obey the laws of that country.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Civil unrest overseas is given as an example of
options_en: a reason citizenship can be cancelled
a time of need for consular help
a crime that is tried by a jury
explanation_en: Part 2 names civil unrest and natural disasters as emergencies in which citizens overseas can seek help from Australian officials.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: A citizen's child born overseas can become an Australian citizen
options_en: only after living in Australia for ten years
by descent, on application
only if born in a Commonwealth country
explanation_en: Part 2 says Australian citizens can apply for their child born overseas to become an Australian citizen by descent.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

stem_en: Active citizens are described as people who
options_en: serve in the Defence Force
hold a job in government
take part in shaping Australia's future
explanation_en: Part 2 says active citizens take on the responsibility and privilege of shaping Australia's future.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Which is an example of participating in Australian society?
options_en: Avoiding all political discussion
Paying tax only when asked
Volunteering for community work
explanation_en: Part 2 lists volunteering for social and community work as one way to participate actively in society.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Paying tax is
options_en: required by law
only for people born in Australia
voluntary for citizens
explanation_en: Part 2 says paying tax is an important way to contribute to the community and is required by law.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Which agency collects tax in Australia?
options_en: The Australian Electoral Commission
The Australian Taxation Office
Services Australia
explanation_en: Part 2 explains that tax is collected by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Tax is paid on money earned from
options_en: overseas sources only
a job, a business or investments
wages from full-time employment only
explanation_en: Part 2 says tax is paid out of the money you earn, whether from a job, a business or investments.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Besides income, taxes are also charged on
options_en: many goods and services
applying for a passport
voting in elections
explanation_en: Part 2 notes that as well as tax on income there are taxes on many goods and services.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: The ATO works to make sure citizens
options_en: know their tax rights and obligations
are correctly enrolled on the electoral roll
vote in every election
explanation_en: Part 2 says the ATO works to ensure all citizens are aware of their tax rights and obligations.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Which of these is paid for with taxes?
options_en: Government-funded healthcare and education
Private sporting club fees
Membership fees for political parties and clubs
explanation_en: Part 2 says taxes pay for services including government-funded healthcare and education, defence, roads and railways, and social security.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: Which levels of government collect taxes to pay for services?
options_en: Federal, state or territory and local
The Australian Government in Canberra only
Local councils only
explanation_en: Part 2 says that as well as the ATO collecting tax, state and territory governments and local councils also collect taxes to pay for services.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society

stem_en: You become an Australian citizen when you
options_en: make the pledge at a citizenship ceremony
pass the citizenship test
receive your first Australian passport in the mail
explanation_en: The booklet's message to you explains that you do not become a citizen until you make the pledge of commitment at a citizenship ceremony.
guideRef: A message to you — The Australian citizenship ceremony

stem_en: Which words in the Australian Citizenship Pledge are optional?
options_en: 'whose laws I will uphold'
'I pledge my loyalty'
'under God'
explanation_en: The booklet's message to you gives the pledge and notes that the words 'under God' are optional.
guideRef: A message to you — The Australian Citizenship Pledge

stem_en: In the Citizenship Pledge you promise to
options_en: uphold and obey Australia's laws
learn an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language
serve in the Defence Force
explanation_en: The pledge, set out at the start of the booklet, includes a promise to uphold and obey the laws of Australia.
guideRef: A message to you — The Australian Citizenship Pledge

stem_en: The Australian Public Service means
options_en: the Australian Army, Navy and Air Force together
government departments and their employees
volunteers in the community
explanation_en: The glossary defines the Australian Public Service as government departments and the people employed by them.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Medicare, Centrelink and Child Support services are delivered by
options_en: local councils
the Australian Taxation Office
Services Australia
explanation_en: The glossary describes Services Australia as the agency that delivers health, social and welfare payments through Medicare, Centrelink and Child Support.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Social security refers to
options_en: the police, courts and prison system
government pensions and benefits for those in need
private health insurance that employers pay for workers
explanation_en: The glossary defines social security as government pensions or benefits for unemployed, disabled, elderly people and others in need.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A volunteer is someone who
options_en: works for the government
is paid a full wage to work for a charity
gives time without expecting payment
explanation_en: The glossary defines a volunteer as a person who gives their time to a person or organisation without expecting payment.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Being self-sufficient means
options_en: living alone in Australia without any family
having a government job
providing for your own needs without help
explanation_en: The glossary defines self-sufficient as being able to provide for your own needs without the help of other people.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: What does the ATO manage?
options_en: Passports and visas
The tax and superannuation systems
Federal elections and the electoral roll
explanation_en: The glossary says the Australian Taxation Office manages the tax and superannuation systems that fund services for Australians.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: At the citizenship ceremony, you pledge to
options_en: vote for the government of the day
uphold and obey Australia's laws
join an Australian political party
explanation_en: Part 3 opens by reminding you that at the citizenship ceremony you pledge to uphold and obey the laws of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — Government and the law in Australia

stem_en: Citizens aged 18 or over must enrol to vote in
options_en: the elections of local sporting clubs and unions
federal, state and territory elections
elections in their country of birth
explanation_en: Part 3 says citizens aged 18 years or over must enrol to vote in federal, state and territory elections and in referenda.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Who must enrol to vote in Australia?
options_en: All residents aged 16 years or over
Only citizens who own property
Citizens aged 18 years or over
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that Australian citizens aged 18 years or over must enrol to vote.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Besides elections, enrolled citizens must also vote in
options_en: votes to choose the Governor-General
national opinion polls on new laws
referenda on constitutional change
explanation_en: Part 3 says enrolment covers federal, state and territory elections as well as referenda on changes to the Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, citizens have their say by
options_en: choosing judges directly in a public vote
voting for someone to represent them in parliament
electing a new Governor-General every three years
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that citizens have a say on how Australia is governed by voting for a person to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: If you are not correctly enrolled, you
options_en: can still vote by showing a passport
cannot vote in an election
may vote in the Senate election only
explanation_en: Part 3 is clear that if you are not correctly enrolled you are not able to vote in an election.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Sunil turned 18 last month and has not enrolled. On election day he
options_en: can vote if a friend confirms his identity
will not be able to vote
can enrol at the polling place and vote
explanation_en: Part 3 says a person who is not correctly enrolled is not able to vote, so enrolling in time matters.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Voting in Australian elections is
options_en: only for citizens born in Australia
optional for people over 70
compulsory
explanation_en: Part 3 says voting is compulsory in Australian elections and in referenda on constitutional change.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which body conducts federal elections and referendums?
options_en: The Australian Electoral Commission
The Department of Home Affairs in Canberra
The High Court of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 describes the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) as the agency responsible for conducting federal elections and referendums.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: The Australian Electoral Commission is a
options_en: Commonwealth agency
state government department
private company hired by parliament
explanation_en: Part 3 says the AEC is a Commonwealth agency.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which organisation maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll?
options_en: The Australian Taxation Office
The AEC
Services Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says the AEC is responsible for maintaining the Commonwealth electoral roll.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: The AEC is described as
options_en: independent of the government
run jointly by the major parties
part of the Prime Minister's office
explanation_en: Part 3 says the AEC is independent of the government, so no party or politician can direct its decisions.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Voting in an Australian election is by
options_en: a signed ballot paper
a public show of hands
secret ballot
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that voting in an Australian election is by secret ballot.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Because voting is by secret ballot, you can
options_en: choose your candidate freely, without anyone pressuring you
be asked by an election official to explain your choice
be required to vote for the sitting local member
explanation_en: Part 3 says that because voting is by secret ballot, you are free and safe to vote for any candidate.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Who is allowed to know whom you voted for?
options_en: Your employer and your local council office
The candidate who received your vote
No one, unless you choose to tell them
explanation_en: Part 3 says no one is allowed to know whom you voted for unless you choose to tell them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: A party worker outside the polling place asks how you voted. You
options_en: do not have to tell anyone
must report the conversation to the AEC
must answer the question honestly
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that your vote is secret and no one can require you to say whom you voted for.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: If you do not vote and have no good reason, you
options_en: lose your Australian citizenship
may have to pay a fine
are removed from the electoral roll
explanation_en: Part 3 says that if you do not vote in an election and have no good reason, you may have to pay a fine.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Priya forgot to vote in the federal election and has no valid excuse. What may happen?
options_en: She may be sent to prison
She must vote twice next time
She may be fined
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that a person who does not vote without a good reason may have to pay a fine.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Compulsory voting makes sure that
options_en: elections are cheaper for the AEC to run
people have a say in who governs them
only well-informed people cast a vote
explanation_en: Part 3 says compulsory voting is a way to make sure the people have a say in who will govern and represent them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Citizens who are worried about a government policy can
options_en: contact their elected representative
ask the Governor-General to cancel the policy
ask the AEC to overturn the policy
explanation_en: Part 3 says Australian citizens can contact their elected representative to raise concerns about government policy.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives

stem_en: How can Australians have a say in forming laws and policies?
options_en: By writing directly to the High Court
By paying an extra voluntary tax
Through their elected representatives
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that by contacting their representatives, all Australians can have a say in forming the laws and policies of a government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives

stem_en: A citizen tells their MP that a law should be changed. The MP should
options_en: consider what has been suggested
ignore it unless many people agree
refer the citizen to the police
explanation_en: Part 3 says that when a citizen suggests a law needs changing, the elected representative should consider what has been suggested.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives

stem_en: Tom, an Australian citizen, disagrees with a new government policy. He can
options_en: ask the AEC to cancel the policy before the next election
refuse to pay tax until the policy is changed
raise his concerns with his elected representative
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that citizens can contact their elected representative to raise concerns about government policy.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives

stem_en: An election is a process through which citizens
options_en: decide whether to change the Australian Constitution
select the judges of the High Court
choose people to represent them in Parliament
explanation_en: The glossary defines an election as a process through which citizens choose people to represent them in Parliament.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: The electoral roll is
options_en: the list of people registered to vote
the record of past election results
the list of candidates standing for election
explanation_en: The glossary defines the electoral roll as the list of people registered to vote in an election or referendum.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: An electorate is
options_en: a building where votes are counted on election night
a district of voters who elect an MP
a group of senators from one state
explanation_en: The glossary says electorates are districts made up of voters who elect politicians to the House of Representatives.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Electoral districts, divisions and seats are other names for
options_en: electorates
commissions
referendums
explanation_en: The glossary notes that electorates are also called electoral districts, divisions or seats.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Voters in an electorate choose a member of
options_en: their local council
the High Court of Australia in Canberra
the House of Representatives
explanation_en: The glossary explains that voters in an electorate elect politicians to the House of Representatives.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A secret ballot means people vote
options_en: only by post from their registered home address
privately, so no one can pressure them
once every ten years at a referendum
explanation_en: The glossary defines a secret ballot as a system where people vote privately so no one can influence or pressure them.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: The purpose of a secret ballot is to
options_en: stop anyone influencing or pressuring voters
speed up the counting of votes on election night
keep the election result secret for a week
explanation_en: The glossary explains that a secret ballot protects voters from being influenced or pressured.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A commission, such as the AEC, is
options_en: a type of court that hears election disputes
a committee of senior government ministers and advisers
a body of people given an official responsibility
explanation_en: The glossary defines a commission as a group of people with an official responsibility.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Australian elections are organised by
options_en: the party that is in government
the office of the Prime Minister
an independent commission
explanation_en: The glossary notes that an independent commission organises the elections.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A representative is a person who
options_en: writes the rules of the Constitution
acts or speaks for others
counts the votes at an election
explanation_en: The glossary defines a representative as a person who acts or speaks for others.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In a referendum, who votes on the proposed change to the Constitution?
options_en: All Australian voters
Only members of federal parliament
Only the premiers of the six states
explanation_en: The glossary defines a referendum as a vote by all voters on a proposed change to the Australian Constitution.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which of these needs a referendum?
options_en: Changing the Australian Constitution
Changing the Prime Minister mid-term
Changing a local council parking rule
explanation_en: The glossary explains that a referendum is held when a change to the Australian Constitution is proposed.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: What must you do before you can vote in a federal election?
options_en: Be correctly enrolled
Get a letter from your MP
Join a political party
explanation_en: Part 3 says you cannot vote unless you are correctly enrolled.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which statement about Australian elections is correct?
options_en: Voting is optional and done by a public show of hands
Voting is compulsory and by secret ballot
Only citizens aged over 21 may vote
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that voting is compulsory for citizens aged 18 or over and is conducted by secret ballot.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: In a referendum on constitutional change, voting is
options_en: limited to members of parliament
compulsory
optional for all voters
explanation_en: Part 3 says voting is compulsory in Australian elections and also when there is a referendum on constitutional change.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: A new citizen asks why Australia makes voting compulsory. Which answer is correct?
options_en: It helps the AEC finish counting votes faster
It raises money for the government through fines
It makes sure the people choose who represents them
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that compulsory voting makes sure the people have a say in who will govern and represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: A government minister tells the AEC how to run the election. In Australia,
options_en: the AEC cannot be influenced by people in government
the AEC must follow the minister's instructions exactly
the AEC must first ask the Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 says political parties and people in government cannot influence the decisions of the AEC.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Who is able to influence the decisions of the Australian Electoral Commission?
options_en: The party holding the most seats in parliament
No political party or person in government
The Prime Minister, acting alone
explanation_en: The voting section says the AEC is independent of the government and that political parties or people in government cannot influence its decisions.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Besides federal elections, which other national votes does the AEC conduct?
options_en: Local council elections
State parliamentary elections
Referendums
explanation_en: The voting section says the Australian Electoral Commission is responsible for conducting federal elections and referendums and keeping the electoral roll.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: From what age must Australian citizens enrol to vote?
options_en: 16 years
18 years
21 years
explanation_en: The voting section says citizens aged 18 years or over must enrol to vote in federal, state and territory elections and referenda.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: What is the list of people registered to vote called?
options_en: The electoral roll
The Census
The electorate
explanation_en: The glossary defines the electoral roll as the list of people registered to vote in an election or referendum.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In a federal election, enrolled citizens vote for
options_en: judges of the High Court
a person to represent them in parliament
the next Governor-General
explanation_en: The voting section says citizens have a say in how Australia is governed by voting for a person to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: If you choose to tell a friend how you voted, this is
options_en: your choice, since no one may know unless you tell them
an offence under the rules of the secret ballot
allowed only after the official result has been declared
explanation_en: The voting section says no one is allowed to know whom you voted for unless you choose to tell them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which of these is a responsibility of the Australian Electoral Commission?
options_en: Deciding who wins a court case
Choosing the Prime Minister after an election
Conducting federal elections
explanation_en: The voting section describes the AEC as the Commonwealth agency that conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the electoral roll.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which of these is a way of having your say in Australia?
options_en: Contacting your elected representative about a policy
Refusing to enrol to vote as a form of protest
Paying someone else to vote in your place on election day
explanation_en: The section on raising matters with your representatives says citizens can contact their elected representative to raise concerns about government policy.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives

stem_en: Maria is a 40-year-old citizen who has never enrolled. She wants to vote at the next federal election. What must she do?
options_en: Nothing; every citizen is enrolled automatically at 18
Ask her local council to add her name to the list
Enrol with the AEC before the election is held
explanation_en: The voting section says citizens must enrol to vote and that someone who is not correctly enrolled cannot vote in an election.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Which of these is NOT true about voting in Australia?
options_en: You must show your completed ballot to a polling official
Voting is by secret ballot
You may be fined for not voting without a good reason
explanation_en: The voting section describes the secret ballot and the fine for not voting without good reason; nothing requires you to show your vote to anyone.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting

stem_en: Before 1901, Australia was made up of
options_en: two large self-governing territories
six separate British colonies
one united and independent nation
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that before 1901 Australia consisted of six separate, self-governing British colonies.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: Before Federation, each colony
options_en: was self-governing with its own laws
shared a single national constitution
was ruled directly from Canberra
explanation_en: Part 3 says each colony was self-governing and had its own constitution and laws.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: Before Federation, who made laws on defence and immigration?
options_en: Each colony, separately
The High Court of Australia
A national parliament in Melbourne
explanation_en: Part 3 says each colony had its own laws relating to defence, immigration, postage, trade and transport.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: Which problem did the separate colonies cause?
options_en: Postage became free across all colonial borders
Trade between colonies was slow and expensive
There were too many national sporting teams
explanation_en: Part 3 gives expensive, slow trade and transport between the colonies as an example of the difficulties before Federation.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: The separate colonies had
options_en: a single shared army and navy
no laws about trade at all
weak systems of defence
explanation_en: Part 3 notes that the separate colonies had weak systems of defence, one reason people wanted to unite.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: One sign that an Australian national identity was forming before 1901 was
options_en: the first election for the new Australian Parliament
sporting teams representing Australia internationally
the opening of the High Court in Canberra
explanation_en: Part 3 says sporting teams were representing Australia internationally as a national identity began to form.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: Before Federation, an Australian culture was developing through
options_en: the design of the national flag
songs, poems, stories and art
national television and radio
explanation_en: Part 3 says an Australian culture was developing in popular songs, poems, stories and art.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: The colonies united to form the Commonwealth of Australia on
options_en: 1 January 1901
26 January 1788
25 April 1915
explanation_en: Part 3 says that on 1 January 1901 the colonies were united into a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: In 1901 the Australian colonies became
options_en: territories governed from London
separate independent countries
a federation of states
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that at Federation the colonies were united into a federation of states.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: The nation formed at Federation is called
options_en: the Dominion of New Holland
the Commonwealth of Australia
the United Colonies of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says the federation of states formed in 1901 is called the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation

stem_en: Which document sets out the basic rules for governing Australia?
options_en: The Australian Citizenship Pledge
The words of the national anthem
The Australian Constitution
explanation_en: Part 3 describes the Australian Constitution as the legal document that sets out the basic rules for the government of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: The full name of the Australian Constitution is
options_en: the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900
the Australian Federation and Independence Agreement Act
the Charter of the Australian Government
explanation_en: Part 3 gives the formal title as the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: The Australian Constitution was originally passed
options_en: by the first Australian Prime Minister
by a unanimous vote of the High Court
as part of an Act of the British Parliament
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Constitution was originally passed as part of a British Act of Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: The Australian Constitution came into effect in which year?
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Constitution was passed in Britain in 1900 but came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the colonies became one nation.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: When the Constitution came into effect, the colonies became
options_en: part of the United States
six independent countries
one independent nation
explanation_en: Part 3 says that when the Constitution came into effect, the Australian colonies became one independent nation.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: The Constitution established a national Parliament consisting of
options_en: a Senate and a High Court
a Cabinet of ministers and a Governor-General
a House of Representatives and a Senate
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Constitution established the Parliament of the Commonwealth, consisting of a House of Representatives and a Senate.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: Which court was established by the Australian Constitution?
options_en: The High Court of Australia
The Federal Circuit Court
The Supreme Court of New South Wales
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Constitution established the High Court of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: Which body has the final power to apply and interpret Australia's laws?
options_en: The Senate of Australia
The High Court of Australia
The office of the Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 says the High Court of Australia has the ultimate power to apply and interpret the laws of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: How can the Australian people change the Constitution?
options_en: By voting in a referendum
By electing a new Prime Minister
By writing to the Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the Australian people can change the Constitution by voting in a referendum.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: Who has the power to change the Australian Constitution?
options_en: The judges of the High Court of Australia
The Governor-General alone
The Australian people, by referendum
explanation_en: Part 3 says it is the Australian people, voting in a referendum, who can change the Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: In the 1967 Referendum, Australians voted 'Yes' to
options_en: create a Senate with equal numbers of members from each state
let Aboriginal peoples be counted in the Census
make Canberra the national capital city
explanation_en: Part 3 describes the 1967 Referendum, in which Australians voted to allow Aboriginal peoples to be counted in the Census.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: In the 1967 Referendum, how many Australians voted 'Yes'?
options_en: Just over half of voters
Fewer than 10 per cent
More than 90 per cent
explanation_en: Part 3 says more than 90 per cent of Australians voted 'Yes' in the 1967 Referendum.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: A 'double majority' is needed to
options_en: change the Constitution
elect a new Prime Minister
pass an ordinary law in parliament
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that a referendum needs a double majority for the Constitution to be changed.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: A double majority means
options_en: a majority of voters nationally and in a majority of states
a majority of members in both Houses of the Australian Parliament
two separate referendums with the same 'Yes' result
explanation_en: Part 3 defines the double majority as a majority of voters in a majority of states and a majority of voters across the nation.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: A referendum wins a national majority of 'Yes' votes, but only two states vote 'Yes'. The result is
options_en: the High Court decides the outcome
the Constitution is not changed
the Constitution is changed immediately
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that both a national majority and a majority in a majority of states are needed, so the change fails.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: For a referendum to succeed, how many states must have a majority of 'Yes' voters?
options_en: At least one state and one territory
A majority of the states
All six states without exception
explanation_en: Part 3 says a change needs a majority of voters in a majority of states as well as a national majority.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: The Constitution divides the power of government into
options_en: federal, state and local powers
royal, religious and military powers of the Crown
legislative, executive and judicial powers
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Constitution divides government power between the legislative, executive and judicial powers.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Why does the Constitution divide the power of government?
options_en: To give the King more control over Australia
To make the law harder for ordinary people to understand
To stop one person or group holding all the power
explanation_en: Part 3 explains the powers are divided to stop one person, or one group, from holding all the power.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Legislative power is the power to
options_en: enforce laws
interpret laws
make laws
explanation_en: Part 3 defines legislative power as the power to make laws.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which body holds legislative power in Australia?
options_en: The Cabinet
Parliament
The High Court
explanation_en: Part 3 says Parliament has the power to make and change the laws in Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: The Australian Parliament is made up of
options_en: ministers chosen by the Governor-General
representatives elected by the people
judges appointed by the King
explanation_en: Part 3 says Parliament is made up of representatives who are elected by the people of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Executive power is the power to
options_en: put the laws into practice
interpret and apply the laws
make and change the laws
explanation_en: Part 3 defines executive power as the power to put the laws into practice.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which of these is part of the Executive?
options_en: The Prime Minister
The Opposition
The High Court of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Executive includes the Prime Minister, Australian government ministers and the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: The Executive includes the Prime Minister, government ministers and
options_en: the judges of the courts
the Governor-General
the Leader of the Opposition
explanation_en: Part 3 lists the Prime Minister, government ministers and the Governor-General as members of the Executive.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Government ministers are responsible for
options_en: the electoral roll
the courts and their judges
government departments
explanation_en: Part 3 says ministers are responsible for government departments.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Judicial power is held by
options_en: ministers
senators
judges
explanation_en: Part 3 says judges have the power to interpret and apply the law, which is the judicial power.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Judicial power is the power to
options_en: make new laws for the nation
interpret and apply the law
collect taxes for the government
explanation_en: Part 3 describes judicial power as the power of judges to interpret and apply the law.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Courts and judges in Australia are
options_en: independent of parliament and government
controlled by the Prime Minister of the day
elected by the people every three years
explanation_en: Part 3 says courts and judges are independent of parliament and government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: A minister wants a judge to decide a case in a particular way. In Australia,
options_en: the Governor-General decides the case instead
the judge must follow the minister's instruction
courts and judges are independent of government
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that courts and judges are independent of parliament and government, so ministers cannot direct them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: The three powers of government are written into
options_en: the words of the national anthem
the Australian Citizenship Pledge
the Australian Constitution
explanation_en: Part 3 says the legislative, executive and judicial powers are written into the Australian Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: The Australian Constitution is best described as
options_en: the supreme law of Australia
a guide to Australian values
a history of the colonies
explanation_en: The glossary defines the Constitution as the supreme law of Australia by which the government must abide.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Who must abide by the Constitution?
options_en: Only new citizens
The government
Only the courts
explanation_en: The glossary says the Constitution is the supreme law by which the government must abide.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which word describes the union of colonies into one nation?
options_en: Referendum
Federation
Constitution
explanation_en: The glossary defines Federation as the union of colonies into one nation, with the colonies retaining certain powers.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Under Federation, the former colonies
options_en: kept certain powers as states
gave up all their powers to Canberra
became territories of the Commonwealth
explanation_en: The glossary explains that in a federation the colonies retain certain powers while uniting as one nation.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which power do the Prime Minister and the Cabinet exercise?
options_en: Executive power
Judicial power
Legislative power
explanation_en: Part 3 gives the Prime Minister and the Cabinet as examples of the executive power, which puts the laws into practice.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: In which year did the British Parliament pass the Act that contains the Australian Constitution?
explanation_en: The Constitution section says the Australian Constitution was originally passed as part of a British Act of Parliament in 1900, before coming into effect in 1901.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: Which event made the Australian colonies one independent nation on 1 January 1901?
options_en: The opening of the first High Court building
The appointment of the first state governors
The Australian Constitution coming into effect
explanation_en: The Constitution section says that on 1 January 1901 the Constitution came into effect and the colonies became one independent nation, the Commonwealth of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: A proposed change to the Constitution wins a majority of voters nationally and majorities in four of the six states. What is the result?
options_en: It fails, because every state must vote 'Yes'
It fails, because two-thirds of states are needed
It passes, because it has a double majority
explanation_en: The Constitution section explains the double majority: a majority of voters in a majority of states plus a majority of voters across the nation.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: Which of these is an example of legislative power?
options_en: Parliament making and changing laws
Judges interpreting the law
Ministers running government departments
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power says legislative power is the power to make laws, held by Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which of these belongs to the judicial power rather than the executive?
options_en: Running a government department
Deciding in court what a law means
Putting a newly passed law into practice
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power says judges hold the power to interpret and apply the law, while the Executive puts laws into practice.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which arm of government includes the Governor-General?
options_en: The courts
The Parliament
The Executive
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power says the Executive includes the Prime Minister, government ministers and the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which of these bodies is made up of representatives elected by the people of Australia?
options_en: The High Court
The Australian Defence Force
The Parliament
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power says Parliament is made up of representatives who are elected by the people of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: The High Court of Australia was established by
options_en: the first Prime Minister
the Australian Constitution
a vote of the state premiers
explanation_en: The Constitution section says the Constitution established the High Court of Australia, which has the ultimate power to apply and interpret Australia's laws.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

stem_en: So that no single person or group ends up with all the power, the Australian Constitution
options_en: divides government power between three arms
gives all power to the Governor-General
lets the High Court run the government
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power says the Constitution divides power between the legislative, executive and judicial arms for exactly this reason.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Which of these is NOT one of the three powers the Constitution divides government into?
options_en: Legislative power
Electoral power
Judicial power
explanation_en: The section on controlling government power names the legislative, executive and judicial powers; there is no 'electoral power' in the Constitution's division.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?

stem_en: Australia's Head of State is
options_en: the Governor-General of Australia
the King of Australia
the Prime Minister of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says Australia's Head of State is the King of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: Who is Australia's current Head of State?
options_en: The Governor-General
The Prime Minister
King Charles III
explanation_en: Part 3 names Australia's Head of State as the King of Australia, His Majesty King Charles III.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: Who appoints the Governor-General?
options_en: The judges of the High Court of Australia
The King, on the Prime Minister's advice
The Australian people, at a federal election
explanation_en: Part 3 says the King appoints the Governor-General as his representative in Australia, on advice from the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: The Governor-General is appointed on the advice of
options_en: the Leader of the Opposition
the Chief Justice of the High Court
the Australian Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the King appoints the Governor-General on advice from the Australian Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: The King appoints the Governor-General to act as
options_en: his representative in Australia
the leader of the Australian Government
the head of the British Parliament in Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says the King of Australia appoints the Governor-General as his representative in Australia, on advice from the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: In relation to political parties, the Governor-General
options_en: acts independently of all of them
gives advice to the Opposition parties
leads the party that is in government
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General acts independently of all political parties.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: What day-to-day role does the King have in Australia's government?
options_en: None
He signs every new law in person
He chairs Cabinet meetings
explanation_en: Part 3 says the King does not have a day-to-day role in government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: In each Australian state, the King is represented by
options_en: a Premier
a Chief Minister
a Governor
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in each state there is a governor who represents the King.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: A state governor's role is similar to that of
options_en: a local council Mayor
the Governor-General
the Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 says each state governor represents the King in a role similar to the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: Australia's system of government is a
options_en: constitutional monarchy
republic with an elected president
absolute monarchy
explanation_en: Part 3 says Australia is a constitutional monarchy.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: In a constitutional monarchy, the King
options_en: can change the Constitution whenever he chooses
must act in accordance with the Constitution
rules without any parliament at all
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that in Australia's constitutional monarchy the King is Head of State but must act in accordance with the Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: Why are the King's powers delegated to the Governor-General?
options_en: Because the Constitution forbids the King from visiting
Because the King is not allowed to vote in Australia
Because the King does not live in Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says that as the King does not live in Australia, his powers are delegated to the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: In Australia, the King's powers are exercised by
options_en: the High Court
the Prime Minister and Cabinet
the Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 says the King's powers are delegated to the Governor-General in Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: Australia's parliamentary democracy reflects traditions from
options_en: China and Japan
Britain and North America
France and Germany in Europe
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Australian system reflects British and North American traditions combined in a uniquely Australian way.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: The leader of the Australian Government is
options_en: the Prime Minister
the Governor-General
the King of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in the Australian system the leader of the Australian Government is the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — Constitutional monarchy

stem_en: The Governor-General is
options_en: not part of the government
a senior member of the Cabinet
the leader of the governing party
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General is not part of the government and must remain neutral.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: In political matters, the Governor-General must remain
options_en: neutral
loyal to the Prime Minister
a member of a political party
