explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General must remain neutral.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Signing Bills passed by Parliament into law is called
options_en: the Opening of Parliament
Royal Assent
a constitutional referendum
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the Governor-General signs all Bills passed by Parliament into law, which is called Royal Assent.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Who gives Royal Assent to Bills passed by the Australian Parliament?
options_en: The Speaker of the House
The Governor-General
The Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 lists signing Bills into law (Royal Assent) as one of the Governor-General's duties.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Which of these is a duty of the Governor-General?
options_en: Deciding cases in the High Court
Performing ceremonial duties
Leading the Opposition in parliament
explanation_en: Part 3 lists performing ceremonial duties among the Governor-General's roles.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Who approves the appointment of federal judges?
options_en: The Leader of the Opposition
The Chief Justice
The Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General approves the appointment of the Australian Government and its ministers, federal judges and other officials.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: The Governor-General approves the appointment of
options_en: the senators elected for each state and territory
the Premiers of each Australian state
the Australian Government and its ministers
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General approves the appointment of the Australian Government and its ministers.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Who starts the process for a federal election?
options_en: The Governor-General
The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Australian Electoral Commission
explanation_en: Part 3 lists starting the process for a federal election among the Governor-General's duties.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Who acts as Commander-in-Chief of Australia's Defence Force?
options_en: the Governor-General
the Prime Minister
the Minister for Defence
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General acts as Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: The Governor-General's reserve powers
options_en: are used in the running of government every day
can only be used in specific circumstances
are shared equally with the Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General has special 'reserve powers' that can only be used in specific circumstances.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: The special powers held by the Governor-General are known as
options_en: royal prerogatives
reserve powers
executive orders
explanation_en: Part 3 calls the Governor-General's special powers 'reserve powers'.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Which statement about the Governor-General is correct?
options_en: The Governor-General leads the Cabinet and the governing party
The Governor-General does not belong to the government
The Governor-General is elected by voters every three years
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the Governor-General is not part of the government and must remain neutral.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: In Australia, a Governor is
options_en: the elected leader of a local government area
the leader of a state government
the Head of State's representative in a state
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders describes a Governor as the representative of the Head of State in each Australian state.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: The leader of a state government is called
options_en: the Governor
the Chief Minister
the Premier
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders says a Premier is the leader of a state government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: The leader of a territory government is called
options_en: the Premier
the Chief Minister
the Territory Administrator
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders says a Chief Minister is the leader of a territory government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: A government minister is
options_en: a judge appointed by the Governor-General to a federal court
an official who organises elections for the AEC
an MP chosen to take charge of an area of government
explanation_en: Part 3 describes a government minister as a Member of Parliament chosen by a government leader to be responsible for an area of government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Who chooses a Member of Parliament to become a government minister?
options_en: A government leader
The High Court
The voters, directly
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders says a minister is chosen by a government leader.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: A Member of Parliament (MP) is
options_en: an elected member of a local government council
an appointed adviser to the King
an elected representative of the people

stem_en: A Senator is an elected representative of
options_en: a political party in the House of Representatives
a local council area in a state parliament
a state or territory in the national Parliament

guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: The leader of a local government is
options_en: a Mayor or Shire President
a Senator for the local area
a Premier
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders says a Mayor or Shire President is the leader of a local government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: An elected member of a local council is called
options_en: a Councillor
a local Minister
a Senator
explanation_en: Part 3's table of leaders says a Councillor is an elected member of a local council.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Which leader is elected to represent a whole state in the Australian Parliament?
options_en: A Governor
A Senator
A Premier
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that a Senator is the elected representative of a state or territory in the Australian Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: A constitutional monarchy is a country where
options_en: an elected president serves as head of state for life
the Prime Minister is both head of state and head of government
a king or queen's powers are limited by the Constitution
explanation_en: The glossary defines a constitutional monarchy as a country in which a king or queen is head of state with powers limited by the Constitution.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: In Australia, what limits the King's powers?
options_en: The Constitution
A vote of the Senate
The Prime Minister's approval
explanation_en: The glossary explains that in a constitutional monarchy the monarch's powers are limited by the Constitution.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: After an election, who approves the appointment of the new Prime Minister?
options_en: The Governor-General
The King, in person
The Leader of the Opposition
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General approves the appointment of the Australian Government and its ministers.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Besides Mayor, what title can the leader of a local government have?
options_en: Shire President
Administrator
Premier
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders names the Mayor or Shire President as the leader of a local government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Who represents the Head of State in the state of Queensland?
options_en: The Premier of Queensland
The Governor of Queensland
The Administrator of Queensland
explanation_en: The Head of State section says that in each state there is a governor who represents the King, in a role similar to the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: Which leader is an MP picked by the head of a government to take charge of one area of government?
options_en: A Senator
A Councillor
A government minister
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders defines a government minister as an MP chosen by a government leader to be responsible for an area of government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: A Chief Minister is the leader of which kind of government?
options_en: A territory government
A state government
A local council
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders says the Chief Minister is the leader of a territory government, while a Premier leads a state government.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: When carrying out the role, the Governor-General acts independently of
options_en: the Australian Constitution
the King
all political parties
explanation_en: The Head of State section says the Governor-General acts independently of all political parties.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?

stem_en: An elected representative of the people in a state parliament is called
options_en: a Member of Parliament
a Governor
a Councillor
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders defines a Member of Parliament as an elected representative of the people in the Australian Parliament or a state parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Which of these leaders is elected rather than appointed?
options_en: The Governor-General
A Senator
A state Governor
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders describes a Senator as an elected representative, while the King appoints the Governor-General and governors represent the King.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Which of these is a role of the Governor-General rather than the Prime Minister?
options_en: Leading the Australian Government
Recommending who should become a minister
Giving Royal Assent to Bills
explanation_en: The section on the Governor-General's role says the Governor-General signs Bills into law (Royal Assent), while the Prime Minister leads the government.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: Which of these is a local government leader?
options_en: A Mayor
A Premier
A Chief Minister
explanation_en: The list of Australia's leaders names the Mayor or Shire President as the leader of a local government; Premiers and Chief Ministers lead states and territories.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

stem_en: Which of these is NOT a role of the Governor-General?
options_en: Serving as Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Force
Leading the political party that is in government
Starting the process for a federal election
explanation_en: The section on the Governor-General's role lists Royal Assent, ceremonial duties, approving appointments, starting elections and the Commander-in-Chief role; the Governor-General is not part of government and must remain neutral.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

stem_en: The Australian Government is also known as
options_en: the Federal or Commonwealth Government
the Local or Municipal Government
the Government of the States and Territories
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Australian Government is also called the Federal Government or the Commonwealth Government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is Australia governed? — The Australian Government

stem_en: How many Houses does the Australian Parliament have?
options_en: Two
One
Three
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Australian Parliament has two Houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is Australia governed? — The Australian Government

stem_en: The two Houses of the Australian Parliament are
options_en: the High Court and the House of Representatives
the House of Representatives and the Senate
the Cabinet and the Senate of Australia
explanation_en: Part 3 names the two Houses of the Australian Parliament as the House of Representatives and the Senate.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is Australia governed? — The Australian Government

stem_en: In a federal election, citizens vote for representatives in
options_en: both Houses of Parliament
the Senate and the High Court
the House of Representatives only
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in a federal election citizens vote to elect representatives to each House of Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is Australia governed? — The Australian Government

stem_en: The House of Representatives is also called
options_en: the People's House or the Lower House
the States' House or the Federal House
the Upper House or the House of Review
explanation_en: Part 3 says other names for the House of Representatives are the Lower House or the People's House.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: For the House of Representatives, Australia is divided into
options_en: provinces
shires
electorates
explanation_en: Part 3 says Australia is divided into federal electorates, each represented by a Member of Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: A Member of Parliament in the House of Representatives represents
options_en: the Governor-General
the whole of their state or territory
the people in their electorate
explanation_en: Part 3 says Members of Parliament (MPs) represent the people in their electorate.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: How is each state or territory's number of MPs decided?
options_en: By the size of the state's land area
By the number of people living there
Each state and territory gets the same number
explanation_en: Part 3 says the number of MPs for each state and territory is based on the number of people living there.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: The House of Representatives has
options_en: about 150 members
exactly 76 members
fewer than 100 members
explanation_en: Part 3 says that overall there are over 150 members elected to the House of Representatives; since the 2025 redistribution the House has exactly 150 seats, so the booklet figure is best read as about 150.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: The role of the House of Representatives includes
options_en: appointing judges to the High Court
debating and voting on proposals for new laws
organising the elections for all local councils
explanation_en: Part 3 says the House of Representatives considers, debates and votes on proposals for new laws and discusses matters of national importance.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: The Senate is also called
options_en: the Lower House
the Upper House
the People's House
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Senate is sometimes called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: Why is the Senate called the States' House?
options_en: Only state Premiers are allowed to sit in it
It meets in a different state capital each year
All states are equally represented in it
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that all states are equally represented in the Senate regardless of their size or population.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: In the Senate, a small state such as Tasmania has
options_en: no senators of its own in the Parliament
the same number of senators as a large state
fewer senators than a large state such as New South Wales
explanation_en: Part 3 says all states are equally represented in the Senate regardless of their size or population.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: How many senators are there in total?
explanation_en: Part 3 says there is a total of 76 senators.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: How many senators does each state elect?
explanation_en: Part 3 says each state elects 12 senators.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: How many senators does the Northern Territory elect?
options_en: Two
None
Twelve
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory elect two senators each.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: How many state governments, each with its own parliament and constitution, does Australia have?
options_en: Six
Eight
Five
explanation_en: Part 3 says there are six states and two mainland territories, and that each state government has its own parliament and constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Each state government has its own
options_en: High Court and Prime Minister
parliament and constitution
King and Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 says each state government has its own parliament and constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: A state government is led by the
options_en: Premier
Chief Minister
Mayor
explanation_en: Part 3 says the leader of a state government is the Premier.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: The Australian Capital Territory government is led by
options_en: a Premier
a Chief Minister
an Administrator
explanation_en: Part 3 says the leader of a territory government is the Chief Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: In each state, who represents the King?
options_en: The Governor-General
A Governor
The Premier
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in each state a Governor represents the King of Australia.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: In the Northern Territory, the Administrator is appointed by
options_en: the Chief Minister of the Territory
the King directly
the Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in the Northern Territory an Administrator is appointed by the Governor-General.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Which have rights recognised by the Constitution?
options_en: Local councils
Territories
States
explanation_en: Part 3 says states have rights recognised by the Constitution while territories do not.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Laws made by a self-governing territory
options_en: can never be changed once they have been passed
must be approved by the High Court of Australia before they apply
can be changed or cancelled by the Australian Government
explanation_en: Part 3 says self-governing territory laws can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government at any time.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Which statement is correct?
options_en: Territory laws cannot be changed by the Australian Government
States need the King's approval for every new law
States can pass laws in their own right
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that states have the power to pass laws in their own right, unlike self-governing territories.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Each local government area has its own
options_en: Governor
council
parliament
explanation_en: Part 3 says each local government area has its own local council.
guideRef: Part 3 — Local government

stem_en: Who elects local councillors?
options_en: The Premier of the state and the Cabinet
The Governor-General
Citizens in the local government area
explanation_en: Part 3 says citizens in each local government area vote to elect their local councillors.
guideRef: Part 3 — Local government

stem_en: Which level of government is responsible for defence?
options_en: The Australian Government
Local governments
State and territory governments
explanation_en: Part 3's list of responsibilities places defence with the Australian Government.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Immigration and citizenship are handled by
options_en: state and territory governments
local councils
the Australian Government
explanation_en: Part 3's list of responsibilities places immigration and citizenship with the Australian Government.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Hospitals and health services are primarily the responsibility of
options_en: local councils
state and territory governments
the Australian Government in Canberra
explanation_en: Part 3 says state and territory governments are primarily responsible for hospitals and health services.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Schools are primarily the responsibility of
options_en: state and territory governments
local councils
the Australian Government in Canberra
explanation_en: Part 3 lists schools among the responsibilities of state and territory governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Rubbish collection is a responsibility of
options_en: the Australian Government
local government
state government
explanation_en: Part 3 lists rubbish collection among the responsibilities of local governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Street signs and traffic controls are the responsibility of
options_en: the Australian Government
the Senate
local councils
explanation_en: Part 3 lists street signs and traffic controls among the responsibilities of local governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Pensions and family support, known as social security, are the responsibility of
options_en: the Australian Government
state and territory governments
local councils
explanation_en: Part 3 lists social security, including pensions and family support, among the Australian Government's responsibilities.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Police and ambulance services are primarily provided by
options_en: local councils
state and territory governments
the Australian Government in Canberra
explanation_en: Part 3 lists police and ambulance services among the responsibilities of state and territory governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Which level of government looks after local libraries and parks?
options_en: State government
Federal government
Local government
explanation_en: Part 3 lists parks, playgrounds and local libraries among the responsibilities of local governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Which of these is a state or territory responsibility?
options_en: Building permits
Public transport
Foreign affairs
explanation_en: Part 3 lists public transport with state and territory governments, foreign affairs with the Australian Government and building permits with local governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: A political party is
options_en: a government department that runs elections
a group sharing ideas about how to govern
a committee of judges who review laws
explanation_en: Part 3 describes a political party as a group of people who share similar ideas about how a country should be governed.
guideRef: Part 3 — What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?

stem_en: Which of these is one of the main political parties in Australia?
options_en: The Federal Union Party
The Australian People's Party
The Australian Greens
explanation_en: Part 3 names the main parties as the Liberal Party of Australia, the Australian Labor Party, the Nationals and the Australian Greens.
guideRef: Part 3 — What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?

stem_en: Parliamentarians who do not belong to a political party are called
options_en: government ministers
independents
senators
explanation_en: Part 3 says parliamentarians who do not belong to any political party are called 'independents'.
guideRef: Part 3 — What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?

stem_en: After a federal election, government is generally formed by
options_en: the party that the Governor-General would prefer to work with
the party that wins the most seats in the Senate
the party holding most seats in the House of Representatives
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Australian Government is generally formed by the party or coalition with the majority of members in the House of Representatives.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: The leader of the party that forms government becomes
options_en: the Governor-General
the Speaker
the Prime Minister
explanation_en: Part 3 says the leader of the party that forms government becomes the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: The Opposition is formed by
options_en: the second largest party in the House of Representatives
the party that lost the most seats at the federal election
the party with the most members in the Senate
explanation_en: Part 3 says the party or coalition with the second largest number of members in the House of Representatives forms the Opposition.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: Who recommends members of parliament to become ministers?
options_en: The Prime Minister
The Leader of the Opposition
The Governor-General
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Prime Minister recommends members of the House of Representatives or Senators to become ministers.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: Who gives approval for the Prime Minister and ministers to be appointed?
options_en: The Governor-General
The King of Australia, in person
The High Court
explanation_en: Part 3 says the Governor-General approves the appointment of the Prime Minister and ministers.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

options_en: an electorate
a shire
a portfolio
explanation_en: Part 3 says a minister's area of government is called a portfolio, giving employment, Indigenous Affairs and the Treasury as examples.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: The Cabinet is made up of
options_en: all elected members of the Australian Parliament
the most senior judges in Australia
ministers with the most important portfolios
explanation_en: Part 3 says ministers with the most important portfolios make up the Cabinet, the key decision-making body of government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: A coalition is
options_en: a committee of the Senate
two or more parties joining together
a group of independent members of parliament
explanation_en: The glossary defines a coalition as the joining of two or more political parties, usually to form a government or opposition.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A shire is
options_en: a local government area
a state parliament
a federal electorate or division
explanation_en: The glossary defines a shire as a local government area.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Where are Australia's state and territory governments based?
options_en: In their own capital cities
In Canberra, alongside the Australian Government
In the largest regional town of each state
explanation_en: Part 3's section on state and territory government says these governments are based in their capital cities.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: In a state or territory election, what do citizens vote to elect?
options_en: A senator to sit in the Australian Parliament in Canberra
The Governor who will represent the King in their state
A representative for their area in the state or territory parliament
explanation_en: The state and territory government section says citizens vote to elect a representative for their area, who becomes a member of the state or territory parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: What names may a local government area have?
options_en: A city, shire, town or municipality
A state, a territory or a region
An electorate, a division or a seat
explanation_en: The local government section says the states and the Northern Territory are divided into local government areas, which may be called cities, shires, towns or municipalities.
guideRef: Part 3 — Local government

stem_en: Local councils are responsible for
options_en: making the criminal law that applies in their area
planning and providing services for their local area
appointing the Governor who represents the King
explanation_en: The local government section says each area has its own council, responsible for planning and delivering services to its local community.
guideRef: Part 3 — Local government

stem_en: The ministers with the most important portfolios together make up
options_en: the Cabinet
the Senate
the Opposition
explanation_en: The section on how the Australian Government is formed says ministers with the most important portfolios make up the Cabinet, the key decision-making body.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the Australian Government formed?

stem_en: Airports and air safety are the responsibility of which level of government?
options_en: The federal (Australian) Government
A state or territory government
A local council
explanation_en: The section on the three levels of government lists airports and air safety among the Australian Government's responsibilities.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Which of these services is handled by local government rather than by a state government?
options_en: Running public hospitals
Police services
Rubbish collection
explanation_en: The section on the three levels of government lists rubbish collection among local government responsibilities, while hospitals and police belong to the states and territories.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: Which of these is true of the Senate but not of the House of Representatives?
options_en: Each state has the same number of members in it
Its members are known as Members of Parliament, or MPs
The party with a majority in it usually forms the government
explanation_en: The Senate section says all states are equally represented in the Senate regardless of size, whereas House seats depend on population and government is formed in the House.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Senate

stem_en: Which name belongs to the House of Representatives rather than to the Senate?
options_en: The House of Review
The People's House
The States' House
explanation_en: The House of Representatives section gives its other names as the Lower House or the People's House; the House of Review and States' House are names for the Senate.
guideRef: Part 3 — The House of Representatives

stem_en: Which of these is true of a self-governing territory but not of a state?
options_en: It has a Governor who represents the King
Its rights are recognised by the Constitution
The Australian Government can alter or revoke its laws at any time
explanation_en: The state and territory government section says states have rights recognised by the Constitution, while territory laws can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government at any time.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government

stem_en: Which of these is NOT a responsibility of the Australian Government?
options_en: Immigration and citizenship
Hospitals and health services
Postal services
explanation_en: The section on the three levels of government lists hospitals and health services as primarily a state and territory responsibility.
guideRef: Part 3 — What do the three levels of government do?

stem_en: In the Australian Parliament, a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law is called
options_en: a Royal Assent.
a Bill.
a referendum.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that when a member of Parliament proposes a new law or a change to an existing one, the proposal is called a Bill.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: Which body can make new laws, or change existing ones, for the whole of Australia?
options_en: The Australian Parliament.
The Australian Federal Police.
The High Court of Australia.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on how laws are made says the Australian Parliament has the power to make or change laws to benefit the nation.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: Before a Bill can be sent to the Governor-General, who must agree to it?
options_en: A majority of members in both Houses of Parliament.
The Prime Minister acting on his or her own.
A majority of the judges sitting on the High Court of Australia.
explanation_en: Part 3 says a Bill goes to the Governor-General only after a majority of members in each House of Parliament have agreed to it.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: The Governor-General's signing of a Bill, which turns it into law, is known as
options_en: a Royal Commission.
a double majority.
Royal Assent.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on how laws are made says the Governor-General's signature on a Bill is called Royal Assent, and this turns the Bill into law.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: Both Houses of Parliament have passed a Bill. What is the next step?
options_en: It goes to the Governor-General to be signed.
It is sent to the High Court for a final ruling.
It is put to the people in a national vote.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that once a majority in each House agrees to a Bill, it goes to the Governor-General, who signs it into law.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: How do the states and territories make their own laws?
options_en: They must ask the Australian Parliament to pass every law on their behalf.
Their parliaments follow a similar process to the Australian Parliament.
Their courts write the laws and the police approve them.
explanation_en: The booklet says state and territory parliaments make their own laws in a similar way to the Australian Parliament.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: Which sequence correctly describes how a federal law is made?
options_en: The Governor-General gives Royal Assent, then the Senate votes on the Bill.
Both Houses pass the Bill, then the Governor-General gives Royal Assent.
The House passes the Bill, then the Prime Minister signs it.
explanation_en: Part 3 sets out the order: the House of Representatives and the Senate debate and vote on a Bill, and only then does the Governor-General sign it, giving Royal Assent.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: A member of Parliament wants to change an existing Australian law. What must she introduce?
options_en: A Bill for Parliament to debate and vote on.
A petition addressed to the Governor-General.
A case in the Federal Court of Australia.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that a member of Parliament who wants a new law or a change to an existing law introduces a Bill, which both Houses then consider.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?

stem_en: Courts in Australia are
options_en: run by the police.
independent.
directed by the Prime Minister.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the courts in Australia are independent and decide cases only on the evidence before them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: On what must an Australian court base its decision?
options_en: The wishes of the government of the day.
Only the evidence presented to it.
Public opinion reported in the media.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on the courts says courts can only base their decisions on the evidence before them.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Who is the highest authority in an Australian court?
options_en: The judge or magistrate.
The police officer who made the arrest.
The lawyer for the accused person.
explanation_en: Part 3 says the judge or magistrate is the highest authority in a court and is independent.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Who can tell an Australian judge or magistrate what to decide in a case?
options_en: The Prime Minister of the day.
The minister who appointed them to the court.
No one, because they are independent.
explanation_en: The booklet says judges and magistrates are independent and no one can tell them what to decide.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: The government disagrees with a judge's decision. Can it take away the judge's job because of this?
options_en: No, the government cannot remove judges for their decisions.
Yes, the government can dismiss the judge immediately for it.
Yes, but only after the next federal election.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that although the government appoints judges and magistrates, it cannot take their jobs away if it disagrees with their decisions.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: In Australia's court system, a person accused of a crime is treated as
options_en: innocent until found guilty in court.
guilty until they prove they are innocent.
guilty if the police say they are.
explanation_en: The booklet says people in Australia are considered innocent until they are found guilty in a court.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Every person appearing in an Australian court has the right to
options_en: be represented by a lawyer.
choose the judge who hears their case.
set their own penalty if found guilty.
explanation_en: Part 3 states that every person has the right to be represented by a lawyer in court.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: What is the role of a jury in an Australian court?
options_en: To decide whether a person is innocent or guilty.
To decide the penalty once a person is found guilty.
To explain the law to the judge.
explanation_en: The booklet says the role of a jury is to decide in court whether a person is innocent or guilty.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Who sits on a jury in Australia?
options_en: Lawyers selected by the government for each individual court case.
Ordinary citizens randomly chosen from the general population.
Police officers from the local police station.
explanation_en: Part 3 describes a jury as a group of ordinary Australian citizens randomly chosen from the general population.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: During a trial with a jury, who explains the law to the jury?
options_en: The judge.
The police prosecutor.
The accused person's lawyer.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on juries says the judge explains the law to the jury.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: In a criminal trial, the jury finds the accused guilty. Who decides the penalty?
options_en: The jury.
The arresting police officer.
The judge.
explanation_en: Part 3 says that in a criminal trial, if the jury finds a person guilty, the judge decides the penalty.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: In an Australian criminal trial with a jury, which statement is correct?
options_en: The judge decides guilt and the jury decides the penalty.
The jury decides both guilt and the penalty.
The jury decides guilt and the judge decides the penalty.
explanation_en: The booklet separates the two roles: the jury decides whether the person is guilty, and the judge then decides the penalty.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: A magistrate is
options_en: a judge of a lower court.
a senior police officer.
a member of Parliament who drafts laws.
explanation_en: The glossary to the testable section defines a magistrate as a judge of a lower court.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: What is the job of the police in Australia?
options_en: To make new laws for the whole community.
To decide whether an accused person is guilty of a crime.
To protect life and property and keep peace and order.
explanation_en: Part 3 says the police maintain peace and order in the community and that their job is to protect life and property.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: In Australia, the police are
options_en: a committee of the Australian Parliament.
independent of the government.
controlled by the Prime Minister's office.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on the police states that the police are independent of the government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: If the police believe someone has broken the law, what can they do?
options_en: Decide the person's guilt and set the punishment.
Arrest the person and bring them before a court.
Send the person to prison without a court hearing.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that the police can arrest a person they believe has broken the law and bring them before a court of law.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: A police officer gives evidence at a trial. Who decides whether the accused is guilty?
options_en: The police officer.
The Minister for Home Affairs.
The court.
explanation_en: The booklet says the police may give evidence in court, but it is the court that decides if a person is guilty or not.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: A crime is committed against the laws of a state. Which police force normally deals with it?
options_en: The Australian Federal Police.
That state's own police force.
The Australian Defence Force.
explanation_en: Part 3 says the states and the Northern Territory have their own police forces, which deal with crimes under state and territory laws.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: The Australian Federal Police investigates crimes against
options_en: state traffic laws, such as speeding offences.
federal laws, such as drug trafficking.
local council rules, such as parking.
explanation_en: The booklet says the AFP investigates crimes against federal laws, for example drug trafficking, crimes against national security and crimes against the environment.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: Which organisation provides everyday policing in the Australian Capital Territory?
options_en: The New South Wales Police Force.
The ACT has no police service of any kind.
The Australian Federal Police.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that, as well as investigating federal crimes, the AFP is responsible for general police work in the Australian Capital Territory.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: A driver stopped by police offers the officer $200 to forget the offence. In Australia this is
options_en: acceptable if the officer agrees to take it.
a crime only if the officer actually accepts the money.
a crime, even if the officer refuses the money.
explanation_en: The booklet says it is a serious crime to bribe the police, and a crime even to offer a bribe to a police officer.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: Where can you report a crime or ask for help in Australia?
options_en: The Governor-General's office.
Your local police.
Your local member of Parliament.
explanation_en: Part 3 says the police and the community have a good relationship, and you can report crimes and seek assistance from your local police.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: Which of these has its own police force that deals with crimes under its own laws?
options_en: The Australian Capital Territory.
The Northern Territory.
Neither of the two mainland territories.
explanation_en: The booklet says the states and the Northern Territory have their own police forces, while the Australian Federal Police does general policing in the ACT.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: You break an Australian law you had never heard of. What can happen?
options_en: Nothing happens, because you did not know about the law at the time.
You receive only a written warning, by law.
You can still be charged; not knowing the law is no excuse.
explanation_en: Part 3 says that if you break an Australian law you did not know about, you could be charged, as not knowing the law is no excuse.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: Which of the following is one of the most serious crimes in Australia?
options_en: Dangerous driving of a motor car.
Disagreeing with a government decision.
Changing from one religion to another.
explanation_en: The booklet's list of the most serious crimes includes murder, assault, armed robbery, fraud, possession of illegal drugs and dangerous driving of a motor car.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: Violence within the home or within a marriage is known in Australia as
options_en: domestic or family violence.
a private matter for the family.
a civil disagreement.
explanation_en: Part 3 explains that violence within the home and within marriage is called domestic or family violence, and it is a very serious crime.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: A man stops his wife seeing her friends and threatens the children to control her. In Australia this is
options_en: domestic and family violence, which is illegal.
acceptable because it happens within a marriage.
only a crime if he physically hits her.
explanation_en: The booklet says domestic and family violence includes isolating a family member from friends and family and threatening children or pets, and it is against the law.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: Who can be sent to jail for committing domestic or family violence in Australia?
options_en: Only a man can be jailed.
A man or a woman.
Only a woman can be jailed.
explanation_en: Part 3 says a person who commits these crimes can go to jail, whether they are a man or a woman.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: You believe a neighbour is in danger from a violent partner. What should you do?
options_en: Wait for the family to sort it out themselves.
Do nothing, because it is a private matter.
Contact the police.
explanation_en: The booklet says that if you or someone you know is in danger, you should contact the police.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: In Australia, road and traffic rules are controlled by
options_en: the Australian Federal Police in Canberra.
state and territory governments.
local councils and shire authorities.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on traffic offences says road and traffic rules are controlled by state and territory governments.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: What do you need before you can legally drive a car in Australia?
options_en: An overseas driver's licence only, with no registration.
Car insurance only; no licence is needed.
A local driver's licence and a registered car.
explanation_en: Part 3 says that to drive a car in Australia you must have a local driver's licence and the car must be registered.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: Who must wear a seatbelt when travelling in a car in Australia?
options_en: Only the driver.
Only passengers in the front seats.
Everybody in the car.
explanation_en: The booklet says everybody travelling in a car must wear a seatbelt.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: How must babies and young children travel in a car in Australia?
options_en: On an adult's lap.
In the front passenger seat.
In an approved car seat.
explanation_en: Part 3 says babies and young children must be in an approved car seat.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: After drinks at a party, a man is over the blood alcohol limit but drives home because it is close. In Australia this is
options_en: allowed for short trips.
allowed if he drives slowly.
illegal.
explanation_en: The booklet says traffic laws are very strict and it is illegal to drive after taking drugs or when above the blood alcohol limit.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: Using a hand-held mobile phone while driving in Australia is
options_en: allowed at low speeds.
against the law.
allowed for phone calls only.
explanation_en: Part 3 says it is against the law to use a hand-held mobile device while driving.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: A criminal trial is
options_en: a court hearing to decide if someone is guilty of a crime.
a meeting of Parliament to debate a proposed criminal law.
an interview with a suspect held at a police station.
explanation_en: The glossary to the testable section defines a criminal trial as a hearing of facts by a court to decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty of a crime.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: A driver in Australia breaks a traffic law. What can happen to the driver?
options_en: Nothing, because traffic rules are only guidelines.
A warning only; traffic offences carry no penalties.
A fine or even a prison sentence.
explanation_en: Part 3's section on traffic offences says people can be fined or sent to prison for breaking traffic laws.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: What does everyone have the right to experience with their family, friends and loved ones?
options_en: Financial support from the Australian Government
Positive and safe relationships
Shared ownership of the family's property
explanation_en: The criminal offences section says everyone has the right to experience positive and safe relationships with their families, friends and loved ones.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: What should no one in Australia have to accept?
options_en: Being treated badly or harmed
Having to obey the law
Paying tax on their income
explanation_en: The criminal offences section says that no one should accept being treated badly or harmed, and that anyone in danger should contact the police.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: Which crimes are examples of what the Australian Federal Police investigates?
options_en: Parking fines and breaches of local council by-laws
Disputes between neighbours over fences and noise
Drug trafficking and crimes against national security
explanation_en: The police section says the AFP investigates crimes against federal laws, such as drug trafficking, crimes against national security and crimes against the environment.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police

stem_en: What does 'drug trafficking' mean?
options_en: Taking drugs shortly before driving a car
Carrying or buying drugs to sell illegally
Importing prescription medicine without a doctor's approval
explanation_en: The glossary defines drug trafficking as carrying or buying drugs to sell illegally.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: To 'enforce the law' means to
options_en: write new laws in the Australian Parliament
interpret the meaning of the law in a court
make sure that people follow the law
explanation_en: The glossary says enforcing the law means making sure that people follow it, which is what the police do while keeping the peace.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which of these is a traffic offence in Australia?
options_en: Driving after taking drugs
Driving a car that is registered
Wearing a seatbelt as a passenger
explanation_en: The traffic offences section says it is illegal to drive after taking drugs or when above the blood alcohol limit; registration and seatbelts are legal requirements, not offences.
guideRef: Part 3 — Traffic offences

stem_en: Which of these is the role of the jury rather than the judge?
options_en: Explaining the law to everyone during the trial
Deciding whether the accused is innocent or guilty
Deciding the penalty once a guilty verdict is reached
explanation_en: The courts section says the jury decides if a person is innocent or guilty, while the judge explains the law to the jury and decides the penalty.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Which of these is a form of domestic or family violence?
options_en: Disagreeing with a partner about household spending
Isolating a partner from their friends and family
Asking a partner to help with the household chores
explanation_en: The criminal offences section says domestic and family violence can include hitting, isolating a family member from friends and family, or threatening children or pets.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia

stem_en: A friend charged with a crime asks whether he must defend himself alone in court. In Australia,
options_en: everyone is entitled to have a lawyer represent them
only Australian citizens may have a lawyer in court
lawyers are allowed only in the High Court
explanation_en: The courts section says every person has the right to be represented by a lawyer in court.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: A newspaper calls an accused person guilty, but no evidence of this is presented at the trial. What must the court do?
options_en: Follow what the newspaper report has said
Ask the government of the day what it should decide
Base its decision only on the evidence before it
explanation_en: The courts section says courts can only base their decision on the evidence before them and are independent of government.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts

stem_en: Australian values are based on
options_en: wealth, social status and family tradition.
freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity.
one shared religion, one language and one common ancestry.
explanation_en: Part 4 opens by saying Australian values are based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values

stem_en: Australian laws apply to
options_en: Australian citizens only, not permanent residents.
people who were born in Australia only.
everyone in Australia, whatever their background.
explanation_en: The introduction to Part 4 says Australian laws apply to all people in Australia, regardless of background or culture.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values

stem_en: A new arrival says the laws of his home country should apply to him in Australia because of his culture. Which is correct?
options_en: He may follow his home country's laws instead of Australia's.
He must follow Australian laws, whatever his background.
Only Australian citizens must follow Australian laws.
explanation_en: Part 4 says that regardless of your background or culture, you must follow Australian laws while in Australia.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values

stem_en: Australian citizenship is about
options_en: keeping your values private and never discussing them in public.
following Australian values only on national holidays.
living out Australian values every day in the local community.
explanation_en: Part 4 explains that citizenship is about living out Australian values in your everyday life and in your local community.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values

stem_en: All people in Australia are expected to
options_en: choose which Australian values apply to them.
respect, share and uphold Australian values.
replace Australian values with their own.
explanation_en: The booklet says it is very important to understand the values that all Australian people are expected to respect, share and uphold.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values

stem_en: A person's 'values' are
options_en: rules written into the Australian Constitution by the founders of the nation.
the prices of goods and services sold in Australian shops.
principles a person uses to decide right from wrong and how to act.
explanation_en: The glossary describes values as the principles that help a person decide what is right and wrong and how to act in various situations.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Under the Rule of Law in Australia,
options_en: nobody, and no group, is above the law.
elected politicians are above the law.
wealthy people can pay to avoid the law.
explanation_en: Part 4 says that under the Rule of Law all Australians are equal in relation to the law and no person or group is above it.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law

stem_en: Late at night the streets are empty and a traffic light is red. What should a driver do?
options_en: Stop, because the law applies even when no one is watching.
Drive through, because nobody is around to see it happen.
Stop only if a police car or speed camera is nearby to catch him.
explanation_en: The booklet's section on the Rule of Law says you should follow the law even if no one is watching.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law

stem_en: A wealthy business owner says the law should not apply to someone as important as him. Which reflects Australian values?
options_en: Important people are exempt from some laws in Australia.
Everyone is equal before the law, including him.
Only the Prime Minister is above the law.
explanation_en: Part 4 explains that all Australians are equal in relation to the law and that no person or group is above the law.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law

stem_en: What happens to people in Australia who break the law?
options_en: They face penalties.
They are only warned the first time.
They are excused if they disagreed with the law.
explanation_en: The booklet says everybody should obey the law and not break it at any time, otherwise they will face penalties.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law

stem_en: A friend says breaking a law is fine as long as you are not caught. Which response matches Australian values?
options_en: Follow the law at all times, watched or not.
It is fine if nobody ever finds out.
You only need to follow the laws you personally agree with.
explanation_en: Part 4 says everybody should obey the law at all times and follow it even if no one is watching.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law

stem_en: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, laws are made by
options_en: parliaments elected by the people.
the police forces of each state.
religious leaders chosen by the community.
explanation_en: Part 4 explains that Australia's laws are determined by parliaments elected by the people.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy

stem_en: Where does the power of the Australian government come from?
options_en: From the King, who personally chooses the members of the government.
From the Australian people, who vote for their representatives.
From the judges of the High Court.
explanation_en: The booklet says the power of the government comes from the Australian people because citizens vote for people to represent them in parliament.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy

stem_en: What does compulsory voting in Australia show?
options_en: The importance of taking part in elections.
That the government does not trust its citizens.
That only some citizens' views matter.
explanation_en: The booklet says voting is compulsory in Australia and that this shows the importance of participating in elections.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy

stem_en: A colleague says he cannot be bothered voting at the federal election. Which is correct?
options_en: Voting is compulsory, so he is expected to vote.
Voting is optional for people who work full time.
Only people born in Australia have to vote.
explanation_en: Part 4 says voting is compulsory in Australia, which shows the importance of participating in elections.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy

stem_en: Because Australia's laws are made by elected parliaments,
options_en: citizens have no say at all in how the country is run.
citizens have a part in how the country is run.
only members of Parliament must obey the laws.
explanation_en: The booklet says that because laws are determined by elected parliaments, Australian citizens are involved in how the country is governed.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy

stem_en: Freedom of speech in Australia means people can express their ideas
options_en: only when the government agrees with them.
only in private, never in public.
freely, provided they stay within the law.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people in Australia should be able to express their ideas freely, so long as it is within the law.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: A newspaper publishes an article strongly criticising a government decision. In Australia this is
options_en: not allowed unless the government approves the article first.
allowed only if the article also praises the government.
allowed; the media have the same free speech as everyone.
explanation_en: The booklet says newspapers, television and radio outlets have the same freedom of speech as individuals.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: Peaceful protest against the actions of the government is
options_en: banned in Australia.
allowed only with the Prime Minister's permission.
allowed and is an essential part of democracy.
explanation_en: Part 4 says Australians are allowed to peacefully protest against government actions because tolerance of peaceful protest is essential to democracy.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: A community group plans a peaceful march against a new government policy. Which is correct?
options_en: They may not march, because it criticises the government.
They may march; peaceful protest is part of democracy.
They may march only if they support the government.
explanation_en: The booklet says Australians are allowed to peacefully protest against the actions of the government.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: Someone posts online urging people to attack members of a religious group. In Australia this is
options_en: never acceptable; it is against Australian values and the law.
acceptable as an exercise of free speech about religion.
acceptable if the person feels very strongly about the religious issue.
explanation_en: Part 4 says it is never acceptable to promote violence against another person or group because of their culture, ethnicity, religion or background.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: A woman posts false allegations about her neighbour on social media. In Australia this is
options_en: protected as free speech.
legal if the neighbour is not a public figure.
illegal.
explanation_en: Part 4 says that it is illegal to make false allegations, even though Australians value freedom of speech.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: At a rally, a speaker urges the crowd to break the law. In Australia this is
options_en: protected as free speech.
legal as long as no one actually breaks the law.
illegal, even though free speech is valued.
explanation_en: The booklet says it is illegal to encourage others to break the law; freedom of speech applies only within the law.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: Your neighbour expresses a lawful political opinion you strongly disagree with. What should you do?
options_en: Report her to the police.
Respect her right to express it.
Demand that she stop talking about politics.
explanation_en: Part 4 says other people's freedom of speech and expression must be respected, as long as it is lawful.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: A group of friends meets in a public park to discuss politics. In Australia this is
options_en: allowed only inside private homes.
allowed only with the government's written permission.
allowed, in public or private places.
explanation_en: Part 4's freedom of speech section says people in Australia are free to meet in public or private places for social or political discussion.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: Which of these is lawful in Australia?
options_en: Making false allegations about another person in the media.
Encouraging other people to break the law.
Writing an article that criticises a government decision.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people may say and write what they think within the law, but making false allegations or encouraging others to break the law is illegal.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech

stem_en: Your cousin wants to join a trade union, but a relative says he needs official permission. Which is correct?
options_en: He needs permission from his employer.
He may only join groups approved by the police.
He is free to join any lawful group he chooses.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people in Australia are free to join any legal organisation, such as a political party, trade union, or religious, cultural or social group.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association

stem_en: Your employer says every staff member must join a particular political party. Which is correct?
options_en: No one can be compelled to join an organisation.
You must join because your employer requires it.
You must join but may leave after one year.
explanation_en: The booklet says individuals cannot be compelled to join an organisation or forced to leave it.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association

stem_en: A friend wants to leave a religious group, but its members say she is not allowed to leave. Which is correct?
options_en: She must stay until the group agrees to release her.
She can leave only with a court order.
She is free to leave; no one can be forced to stay.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people in Australia are free to join or leave any group voluntarily, as long as it is within the law.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association

stem_en: A protest against a company's actions turns into protesters smashing shop windows. In Australia this is
options_en: acceptable, because protest is a democratic right in Australia.
acceptable if the company has done something wrong.
unlawful; protests must be peaceful and not damage property.
explanation_en: The booklet says all protests must be within the law: peaceful, and must not injure any person or damage property.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association

stem_en: All protests in Australia must
options_en: be approved in advance by the Prime Minister and the police.
support the position of the government.
be peaceful and not injure anyone or damage property.
explanation_en: Part 4 says Australians can gather to protest, but all protests must be within the law, peaceful, and must not injure people or damage property.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association

stem_en: A new migrant asks which religion is Australia's official national religion. Which is correct?
options_en: Australia has no official national religion.
Christianity is the official national religion.
Each state and territory chooses its own official religion.
explanation_en: Part 4 says Australia has no official national religion and people are free to follow any religion they choose.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: The Australian government treats its citizens
options_en: more favourably if they belong to a Christian church.
equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.
more favourably if they have no religion.
explanation_en: The booklet says the government treats all citizens equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: In Australia, religious laws
options_en: override Australian law for believers.
apply in areas where most residents share that religion.
have no legal status.
explanation_en: Part 4 says religious laws have no legal status in Australia and Australian law must be followed by everyone.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A religious rule followed by your family is different from an Australian law. Which must be followed in Australia?
options_en: The Australian law.
The religious rule.
Whichever one the family prefers.
explanation_en: The booklet says Australian law must be followed by everyone in Australia, including where it is different from religious laws.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A man who is already married wants to take a second wife while still married to the first. In Australia this is
options_en: allowed if his religion permits more than one wife.
against the law and can lead to imprisonment.
allowed if both wives agree.
explanation_en: Part 4 says polygamy, being married to more than one person at the same time, is against the law and can result in severe penalties, including imprisonment.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A family arranges for their daughter to marry a man against her will. In Australia this is
options_en: acceptable as a cultural or religious tradition of the family.
legal as long as the whole family, including her parents, agrees.
forced marriage, which is illegal and carries severe penalties.
explanation_en: The booklet says forced marriage is against the law in Australia and can result in severe legal penalties, including imprisonment.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Religious intolerance in Australian society is
options_en: not acceptable.
acceptable in private.
acceptable towards minority religions.
explanation_en: Part 4 states that religious intolerance is not acceptable in Australian society.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A colleague refuses to work with someone because of their religion and mocks their beliefs. In Australia this is
options_en: fine, because everyone is entitled to a personal opinion.
acceptable if other colleagues agree.
religious intolerance, which is not acceptable.
explanation_en: The booklet says religious intolerance is not acceptable and that all people should have equal opportunity regardless of their religion.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Your neighbour changes from one religion to another. In Australia she is
options_en: free to follow any religion she chooses.
required to keep the religion of her parents.
required to get government approval first.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people in Australia are free to follow any religion they choose.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: A forced marriage is one where
options_en: the couple were introduced to each other by their families.
at least one of the couple had no free choice.
the couple come from different religions.
explanation_en: The glossary defines forced marriage as a marriage where one or both of the couple did not have a free choice.
guideRef: Glossary of testable section

stem_en: Which statement about religious practices in Australia is correct?
options_en: They are allowed even where they break Australian law.
They are not allowed in public places.
They are allowed if they do not break Australian law.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people are free to follow any religion, but religious practices must not break Australian laws.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion

stem_en: Australian society values equal rights for everyone, regardless of their
options_en: gender, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion or race.
gender and age only, once they become Australian citizens.
religion only, provided they were born in Australia.
explanation_en: Part 4 says Australian society values the equal rights of all people regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, race, or national or ethnic origin.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: Two women want to marry each other in Australia. Which is correct?
options_en: They may not; marriage is only between a man and a woman.
They may marry only with a religious leader's approval.
They may marry; two people of the same sex can marry.
explanation_en: The booklet says that under Australian law two people can marry each other, including two men or two women.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A Buddhist and a Christian face the same charge in an Australian court. How are they treated?
options_en: The Christian is treated more favourably.
In the same way under the law.
The Buddhist is treated more favourably.
explanation_en: Part 4 says people of different backgrounds are neither given preferential treatment nor discriminated against; Buddhists and people of all faiths receive the same treatment as Christians.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: Who is able to join the Australian Defence Force or the police in Australia?
options_en: Men only.
Both men and women.
Women only in support roles.
explanation_en: Part 4 says both men and women can join the Australian Defence Force and the police force.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A manager refuses to promote any woman, no matter how well she performs. In Australia this is
options_en: against the law.
allowed in small businesses.
allowed for senior positions.
explanation_en: The booklet says it is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A woman and a man apply for the same job. She has better qualifications and skills. Which is correct?
options_en: The man should get the job because he is a man.
It is her right to get the job ahead of him.
The job must be shared equally between them.
explanation_en: Part 4 says it is a right for a woman to get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A husband tells his wife she is not allowed to change her religion. Which reflects Australian values?
options_en: The husband decides all religious matters for the whole family.
She has the right to make her own choice about religion.
She needs a court order to change her religion.
explanation_en: The booklet says both men and women have the right to make their own independent choices about personal matters such as marriage and religion.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: Is it acceptable in Australia to hit your partner when you are angry?
options_en: No, never; it is a criminal offence.
Yes, if the partner started the argument.
Yes, as long as there is no serious injury.
explanation_en: Part 4 says physical violence against a spouse or partner is never acceptable and is a criminal offence in Australia.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A wife wants a divorce but her husband wants to stay married. In Australia,
options_en: she must stay married until he agrees to a divorce.
she may apply to the courts for a divorce.
only the husband can apply for a divorce.
explanation_en: The booklet says divorce is acceptable in Australia and either a husband or a wife may apply to the courts, even if the other spouse wishes to continue the marriage.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A man says women should not be allowed to vote. Which is correct in Australia?
options_en: He is correct; only men vote in federal elections.
Men and women have equal rights to vote.
Women may vote only in local council elections.
explanation_en: Part 4 says both men and women can vote at elections and have equal rights in Australia.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: A colleague says people with a disability should not have the same rights as others. Which reflects Australian values?
options_en: Rights depend on how useful a person is to the wider society.
Employers may decide which rights their staff have.
Everyone has equal rights, regardless of disability.
explanation_en: The booklet says Australian society values the equal rights of all people regardless of disability, among other characteristics.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: In Australia, who decides whether a woman marries, and whom she marries?
options_en: The woman herself, as her own independent choice.
Her father or her eldest brother, acting for the family.
Her religious leader.
explanation_en: Part 4 says both men and women have the right to make their own independent choices about personal matters such as marriage.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: In court, a man argues that his evidence should count for more than a woman's. Which is correct in Australia?
options_en: A man's evidence is always given more weight in court.
It depends on the religion of the judge.
Men and women are treated equally in courts of law.
explanation_en: The booklet says men and women are treated equally in courts of law in Australia.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law

stem_en: In Australia, a 'fair go' means
options_en: everyone receives exactly the same income, whatever work they do.
everyone has an equal chance to succeed, whatever their background.
wealthy families always get the first choice of the best jobs and schools.
explanation_en: Part 4 says everyone deserves a fair go and that everyone, regardless of background, is given an equal opportunity to achieve success in life.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: A young woman from a poor family works hard and becomes a doctor. Which Australian value does this reflect?
options_en: That only people from wealthy families should become doctors.
That success depends on who you know.
A fair go: achievement should come from hard work and talent.
explanation_en: The booklet says what someone achieves in life should be a result of their hard work and talents, not class distinctions.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: An employer wants to hire a less skilled applicant because he comes from a wealthy family. Which is correct?
options_en: It is fine to prefer applicants who come from wealthy and well-known families.
It is fine, as long as the wealthy applicant is also a man.
The law backs choosing whoever has the best skills and experience.
explanation_en: Part 4 says that when an organisation fills a job, the law supports selecting the person with the best skills and experience.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: In Australia, a job should go to a person because of
options_en: their skills and experience.
their gender.
their family's wealth or their ethnicity.
explanation_en: The booklet says a person should get a job based on their skills and experience, not because of their gender, wealth or ethnicity.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: Many new migrants in Australia have
options_en: become leaders in business, the arts, public service and sport.
been kept out of leadership roles in most Australian industries.
been limited to low-paid work in farming and factories.
explanation_en: Part 4 says many new migrants have become leaders in business, their profession, the arts, public service and sport through hard work and enterprise.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: In Australia, people should not be held back by
options_en: the need to work hard.
any kind of class distinction.
the need to obey the law like everyone else.
explanation_en: The booklet says everyone deserves a fair go and people should not be limited by any kind of class distinction.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

stem_en: Which statement reflects the Australian idea of a 'fair go'?
options_en: People with wealthy parents always deserve the best jobs and schools.
Success should come from hard work and talent, not social class.
Migrants should not expect to become leaders.
